blocks.body:
In one variable, the fundamental theorem of calculus has a quiet corollary: a function whose derivative vanishes is constant. Already on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ this fails, since a function can be $1$ on the positive half-line and $0$ on the negative one. The failure is caused by the shape of the domain, not by the function. In several variables the same thing happens one degree up. A curl-free vector field on a star-shaped region is a gradient, but on $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus the $z$-axis the field $(-y,x,0)/(x^2+y^2)$ is curl-free and is not a gradient: its line integral around the axis is $2\pi$, while the integral of a gradient around any closed loop is $0$. On $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a point, which is simply connected, every curl-free field is a gradient, but there are divergence-free fields that are not curls.

De Rham cohomology turns these observations into invariants. In each degree $k$ one takes the solutions of $d\omega=0$ (closed forms) and divides out by the solutions that are there for a trivial reason, the forms $d\eta$ (exact forms). The quotient $H^k(M)$ is a real vector space, and its size measures how badly "closed implies exact" fails on $M$. The page [[differential-forms]] ended with the angle form on the punctured plane, which is closed and not exact; that single example already contains the main idea. Here we build the theory: the groups and their ring structure, homotopy invariance, the Mayer–Vietoris sequence, the Künneth formula, and de Rham's theorem identifying $H^k(M)$ with the real singular cohomology dual to [[homology]]. Compactly supported cohomology and Poincaré duality, which are built from these tools, are on the next page, [[poincare-duality|Compact supports and Poincaré duality]]. The later sections give the parts of Hodge theory, characteristic classes, discrete versions and the physics vocabulary that current papers assume.

Throughout, $M$ is a smooth manifold as on [[smooth-manifolds]] (Hausdorff, second countable, so smooth partitions of unity exist), $\Omega^k(M)$ is the real vector space of smooth $k$-forms on $M$, and $d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M)$ is the exterior derivative, with $d\circ d=0$ and $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta$ for $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$. Pullback $F^*$ along a smooth map commutes with $d$ and with $\wedge$. All of this is on [[differential-forms]], where it was done on open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$; on a manifold one works chart by chart, because the coordinate formula for $d$ is compatible with pullback.

blocks.title: Closed forms, exact forms and the de Rham groups
blocks.body:
Because $d\circ d=0$, the spaces of forms and the maps $d$ form a cochain complex, the de Rham complex
$$0\to\Omega^0(M)\xrightarrow{d}\Omega^1(M)\xrightarrow{d}\Omega^2(M)\xrightarrow{d}\cdots\xrightarrow{d}\Omega^n(M)\to0,\qquad n=\dim M.$$
Write $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{k+1})$ for the closed $k$-forms and $B^k(M)=d(\Omega^{k-1}(M))$ for the exact ones, with $B^0=0$. Then $B^k\subseteq Z^k$, which is the statement "exact implies closed" from [[differential-forms]].

Compare the homology page: there a chain complex $C_n$ with $\partial\partial=0$ gave cycles $Z_n$, boundaries $B_n$ and $H_n=Z_n/B_n$. The de Rham complex goes up in degree instead of down (a cochain complex), and its terms are infinite-dimensional real vector spaces rather than finitely generated abelian groups. The quotient construction is the same.

blocks.title: De Rham cohomology
blocks.body:
The $k$-th de Rham cohomology group of $M$ is the real vector space
$$H^k(M)=H^k_{dR}(M)=\frac{Z^k(M)}{B^k(M)}=\frac{\ker\big(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M)\big)}{\operatorname{im}\big(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^{k}(M)\big)}.$$
Its elements are classes $[\omega]$ of closed forms, and $[\omega]=[\omega']$ means $\omega-\omega'=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$; one says $\omega$ and $\omega'$ are cohomologous. The direct sum $H^*(M)=\bigoplus_k H^k(M)$ is graded by degree. When $\dim H^k(M)$ is finite it is called the $k$-th Betti number $b_k(M)$.

In words: closed $k$-forms, where two of them count as the same if they differ by a derivative.

blocks.title: What a de Rham class measures
blocks.body: The definition is short, and the sources read it in noticeably different ways. Each reading is used somewhere later on the page.

items.label: Holes detected by integrals
items.body: Petrov starts from the punctured plane. Over a loop that bounds a disc in the domain, Stokes gives $\int_C\omega=\int_D d\omega=0$ for a closed $\omega$; a loop that is not the boundary of a disc in the domain must enclose a hole, and for the angle form around the puncture the integral is $2\pi$ (the computation of the example below). Since exact forms integrate to zero over every closed loop, a nonzero loop integral certifies that a closed form is not exact, and the number of independent such forms counts holes.

items.label: Solutions modulo obvious solutions
items.body: López Neumann writes the vector-calculus complex $$C^\infty(U)\xrightarrow{\nabla}C^\infty(U,\mathbb{R}^3)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}C^\infty(U,\mathbb{R}^3)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}C^\infty(U)$$ for open $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$. Each equation (zero gradient, zero curl, zero divergence) has obvious solutions coming from the previous operator. The cohomology in each degree is all solutions divided by the obvious ones: $H^1(U)$ is curl-free fields modulo gradients, $H^2(U)$ is divergence-free fields modulo curls.

items.label: Failure of calculus' main theorem
items.body: The same slides credit Tao with the phrase that de Rham cohomology measures how far the fundamental theorem of calculus fails on a general manifold. In degree $0$ the failure is disconnectedness (zero derivative does not force a constant), and in higher degrees it is the failure of a closed form to have a potential.

items.label: Locally trivial, globally not
items.body: By the Poincaré lemma (proved below) every closed form is exact on a small ball, so every class is locally zero. A nonzero class is therefore a purely global object: it records how local potentials fail to glue. Bott and Tu make this the organising principle, computing everything by gluing open sets with the Mayer–Vietoris sequence.

blocks.title: First properties
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold.
1. $H^0(M)$ is the space of locally constant functions. If $M$ has $r$ connected components then $H^0(M)\cong\mathbb{R}^r$; for $M$ connected, $H^0(M)=\mathbb{R}$.
2. $H^k(M)=0$ for $k>n$ (and for $k< 0$).
3. If $M=\bigsqcup_j M_j$ is a disjoint union of open pieces (countably many), restriction gives an isomorphism $H^k(M)\cong\prod_j H^k(M_j)$.

1. There are no exact $0$-forms, so $H^0(M)=Z^0(M)$, the smooth functions with $df=0$. In a chart $df=0$ means all partial derivatives vanish, so $f$ is constant on each connected chart domain, hence locally constant. A locally constant function is constant on each connected component, and any choice of one constant per component is smooth. So $H^0(M)\cong\mathbb{R}^r$.

2. At each point $T_p^*M$ has dimension $n$, and an alternating $k$-linear form on an $n$-dimensional space vanishes when $k>n$ (it is a combination of $dx_I$ with $|I|=k$, and there are none). So $\Omega^k(M)=0$.

3. A form on $M$ is the same as a family of forms on the $M_j$, with no compatibility condition since the pieces are disjoint and open; $d$ acts piece by piece. So $\Omega^*(M)=\prod_j\Omega^*(M_j)$ as complexes, and kernels and images are computed componentwise.

blocks.title: The real line and the circle
blocks.body: (a) Compute $H^*(\mathbb{R})$ directly. (b) On $S^1=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ with angle coordinate $\theta$, the form $d\theta$ is a well-defined closed $1$-form (the differential of the local angle functions, which differ by constants on overlaps) even though $\theta$ is not a function. Show that $H^1(S^1)\cong\mathbb{R}$, with the isomorphism $[\omega]\mapsto\int_{S^1}\omega$, and that $[d\theta]$ is a basis.
blocks.solution:
(a) $\mathbb{R}$ is connected, so $H^0=\mathbb{R}$. Every $1$-form $g(x)\,dx$ is closed (there are no $2$-forms) and is exact: $g\,dx=dG$ with $G(x)=\int_0^xg$. So $H^1(\mathbb{R})=0$, and $H^k(\mathbb{R})=0$ for $k\ge2$ by dimension.

(b) $S^1$ is connected, so $H^0=\mathbb{R}$. Pull a $1$-form back along $t\mapsto t \bmod 2\pi$: it becomes $g(t)\,dt$ with $g$ smooth and $2\pi$-periodic, and $\int_{S^1}\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}g$. Put $c=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}g$ and $f(t)=\int_0^t(g-c)$. Then $f(t+2\pi)-f(t)=\int_t^{t+2\pi}(g-c)=0$, so $f$ is periodic and defines a smooth function on $S^1$ with $df=(g-c)\,d\theta$. Hence $\omega=c\,d\theta+df$: every class is a multiple of $[d\theta]$. Conversely $\int_{S^1}df=0$ for every function $f$ (the integrand $f'$ is a derivative of a periodic function), so the linear map $[\omega]\mapsto\int_{S^1}\omega$ is well defined on classes, and it sends $[d\theta]$ to $2\pi\ne0$. So it is an isomorphism $H^1(S^1)\to\mathbb{R}$ and $[d\theta]\ne0$: $d\theta$ is closed and not exact, because $\theta$ is not a global function.

blocks.title: The punctured plane with two punctures
blocks.body: Let $U=\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{p,q\}$ with $p=(-1,0)$ and $q=(1,0)$. For a point $a$ let $\omega_a$ be the angle form centred at $a$, $$\omega_a=\big(-(y-a_2)\,dx+(x-a_1)\,dy\big)/|z-a|^2$$ where $z=(x,y)$. Show that $[\omega_p]$ and $[\omega_q]$ are linearly independent in $H^1(U)$.
blocks.solution:
Both forms are closed on $U$ (each is the pullback of the closed angle form of [[differential-forms]] under a translation). Let $\gamma_p$ and $\gamma_q$ be circles of radius $\tfrac12$ around $p$ and $q$, traversed counterclockwise. The integral of $\omega_a$ over a circle centred at $a$ is $2\pi$; over a circle not enclosing $a$ it is $0$, because on the disc bounded by that circle $\omega_a$ is closed and Stokes gives $\int_{\partial D}\omega_a=\int_Dd\omega_a=0$. So the period matrix is
$$\begin{pmatrix}\int_{\gamma_p}\omega_p&\int_{\gamma_q}\omega_p\\ \int_{\gamma_p}\omega_q&\int_{\gamma_q}\omega_q\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\pi&0\\0&2\pi\end{pmatrix}.$$
If $\lambda\omega_p+\mu\omega_q=df$ then both loop integrals of $df$ vanish, giving $2\pi\lambda=2\pi\mu=0$. So the classes are independent and $\dim H^1(U)\ge2$. The Mayer–Vietoris section shows that equality holds, so these two classes form a basis.

blocks.caption: The angle form $\omega=(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2)$ on the punctured plane: its integral is $2\pi$ around a loop encircling the missing origin and $0$ around a loop that bounds a disc inside the domain.
blocks.alt: A punctured plane drawn as a region with a hollow dot at the origin. A large counterclockwise circle around the origin is labelled with integral 2 pi; a small circle to the upper right, not enclosing the origin, is labelled with integral 0.

blocks.body:
1. Show that $H^k$ of a point is $\mathbb{R}$ for $k=0$ and $0$ otherwise, and that $H^0(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})\cong\mathbb{R}^2$.
2. On $S^1$, decide whether $\omega=(2+\cos\theta+\sin 3\theta)\,d\theta$ is cohomologous to $2\,d\theta$, and if so find $f$ with $\omega-2\,d\theta=df$.
3. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be open and $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ closed. Show that if $\int_\gamma\omega=0$ for every closed piecewise smooth loop $\gamma$ in $U$, then $\omega$ is exact (define $f(z)=\int_{z_0}^z\omega$ along any path, on each component).
4. Show that the $2$-form $x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy$ on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, divided by $(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, is closed, and use its integral over the unit sphere to show that $H^2(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\})\ne0$.

blocks.title: Products and pullbacks
blocks.body: Two pieces of structure on forms pass to cohomology: the wedge product and pullback. Together they make $H^*$ a contravariant functor from smooth manifolds to graded-commutative rings, which is how the papers treat it (for example Notman–Sanabani regard $H(M;\mathbb{R})$ as a graded algebra from the start, and Gualtieri states functoriality as a corollary of $F^*d=dF^*$).

blocks.title: Ring structure and functoriality
blocks.body:
1. The wedge product induces a well-defined bilinear product $H^k(M)\times H^l(M)\to H^{k+l}(M)$, $[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha\wedge\beta]$. It is associative, has unit $[1]\in H^0(M)$, and is graded commutative: $[\beta][\alpha]=(-1)^{kl}[\alpha][\beta]$.
2. A smooth map $F:M\to N$ induces $F^*:H^k(N)\to H^k(M)$, $F^*[\omega]=[F^*\omega]$, which is a ring homomorphism. Moreover $(G\circ F)^*=F^*\circ G^*$ and $\mathrm{id}^*=\mathrm{id}$. In particular diffeomorphic manifolds have isomorphic cohomology rings.

1. If $\alpha,\beta$ are closed then $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta\pm\alpha\wedge d\beta=0$, so $\alpha\wedge\beta$ is closed. If $\alpha$ is replaced by $\alpha+d\eta$, the product changes by $d\eta\wedge\beta=d(\eta\wedge\beta)$, because $d(\eta\wedge\beta)=d\eta\wedge\beta+(-1)^{k-1}\eta\wedge d\beta$ and $d\beta=0$. Similarly for $\beta$, using $\alpha\wedge d\eta=(-1)^kd(\alpha\wedge\eta)$ when $d\alpha=0$. So the class of $\alpha\wedge\beta$ depends only on the classes. Associativity, the unit and $\beta\wedge\alpha=(-1)^{kl}\alpha\wedge\beta$ hold already for forms.

2. Since $F^*d=dF^*$, $F^*$ maps closed forms to closed forms and exact forms to exact forms ($F^*d\eta=dF^*\eta$), so it is well defined on classes. It respects products because $F^*(\alpha\wedge\beta)=F^*\alpha\wedge F^*\beta$, and the composition rules hold for pullback of forms.

blocks.title: Products on the circle and the torus
blocks.body: (a) Show that $H^*(S^1)\cong\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2)$ with $x=[d\theta]$. (b) On the torus $T^2=S^1\times S^1$ with angle coordinates $\theta_1,\theta_2$, show that $[d\theta_1]\,[d\theta_2]\ne0$ in $H^2(T^2)$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $H^0=\mathbb{R}\cdot1$ and $H^1=\mathbb{R}\cdot x$ by the earlier example, and $x^2=[d\theta\wedge d\theta]=0$ (there are no $2$-forms on a $1$-manifold). So $H^*=\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathbb{R}x$ with $x^2=0$.

(b) The forms $d\theta_1$, $d\theta_2$ are pullbacks of $d\theta$ under the two projections, so they are closed. On a compact oriented manifold without boundary, the integral of an exact top form is zero by Stokes. Here $\int_{T^2}d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta_1\,d\theta_2=4\pi^2\ne0$, so $d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2$ is not exact. Graded commutativity gives $[d\theta_2][d\theta_1]=-[d\theta_1][d\theta_2]$. The Künneth section shows that $1,[d\theta_1],[d\theta_2],[d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2]$ is a basis of $H^*(T^2)$, so the ring is the exterior algebra on two degree-one generators.

blocks.body:
1. Let $F:S^1\to S^1$ be $F(\theta)=m\theta$ for an integer $m$. Compute $F^*$ on $H^1(S^1)$ in the basis $[d\theta]$.
2. Show that if $\alpha$ is a closed form of odd degree then $[\alpha]^2=0$. Give an example of a closed $2$-form $\beta$ on some manifold with $[\beta]^2\ne0$ (try $T^4$).
3. Let $\iota:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$ be the inclusion of the unit circle. Show that $\iota^*$ is an isomorphism on $H^1$ by computing $\iota^*[\omega]$ for the angle form $\omega$. (Homotopy invariance will give a second proof.)

blocks.title: Integration, Stokes and periods
blocks.body:
Two kinds of integration are used constantly in papers: integration of a top-degree form over an oriented manifold, and integration of a $k$-form over a smooth singular $k$-chain. Both were set up on [[differential-forms]]; here is what they do on cohomology.

Smooth singular chains. A smooth singular $k$-simplex is a smooth map $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ from the standard simplex (smooth meaning it extends smoothly to a neighbourhood of $\Delta^k$ in its affine span). Real linear combinations form the smooth chain group $C_k^\infty(M)$, with the boundary $\partial\sigma=\sum_i(-1)^i\sigma\circ F_i$ of [[homology]], where $F_i$ is the $i$-th face inclusion. For a $k$-form $\omega$ one defines $\int_\sigma\omega=\int_{\Delta^k}\sigma^*\omega$ and extends linearly. Stokes' theorem for chains reads
$$\int_c d\eta=\int_{\partial c}\eta\qquad(c\in C^\infty_k(M),\ \eta\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)).$$
Ginory proves it by reducing to one simplex and keeping track of which faces are orientation preserving; the face $F_i$ preserves orientation exactly when $i$ is even, which is where the signs in $\partial$ come from.

Periods. If $\omega$ is closed and $z$ is a smooth cycle ($\partial z=0$), the number $\int_z\omega$ is a period of $\omega$. It depends only on the class $[\omega]$ and on the homology class of $z$: changing $\omega$ by $d\eta$ changes the integral by $\int_z d\eta=\int_{\partial z}\eta=0$, and changing $z$ by a boundary $\partial b$ changes it by $\int_{\partial b}\omega=\int_b d\omega=0$. So integration gives a bilinear pairing
$$H^k(M)\times H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R},\qquad([\omega],[z])\mapsto\int_z\omega,$$
and the de Rham theorem below says it is perfect. The working consequence: to prove that a closed form is not exact, find one cycle on which its integral is nonzero.

blocks.title: Top-degree classes on compact oriented manifolds
blocks.body: Let $M$ be a compact oriented $n$-manifold without boundary. Then integration $\int_M:\Omega^n(M)\to\mathbb{R}$ vanishes on exact forms and so defines a linear map $\int_M:H^n(M)\to\mathbb{R}$. It is surjective; in particular a nowhere-vanishing $n$-form compatible with the orientation (a volume form) represents a nonzero class, and $H^n(M)\ne0$. If $M$ is also connected, $\int_M:H^n(M)\to\mathbb{R}$ is an isomorphism (proved on [[poincare-duality|Compact supports and Poincaré duality]]).

For $\eta\in\Omega^{n-1}(M)$, Stokes with $\partial M=\varnothing$ gives $\int_Md\eta=0$; every form on a compact manifold has compact support. A volume form $\mu$ is positive in every oriented chart, so $\int_M\mu>0$, and scaling $\mu$ hits every real number. The last statement is the case $k=n$ of [[poincare-duality|Poincaré duality]] for connected $M$: $H^n(M)\cong H^0(M)^*=\mathbb{R}$, with the isomorphism given by pairing against the constant function $1$, which is $\int_M$.

blocks.title: A sphere has a nonzero top class, and the class is a flux
blocks.body: Let $\Phi=\dfrac{x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$. Show that $\Phi$ is closed, that $\int_{S_R}\Phi=4\pi$ for the sphere $S_R$ of every radius $R$, and explain why the second fact follows from the first without computing.
blocks.solution:
$\Phi$ is the $2$-form attached to the vector field $F(p)=p/|p|^3$, $p=(x,y,z)$, by the dictionary of [[differential-forms]], so $d\Phi=(\operatorname{div}F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, and $\operatorname{div}F=3/|p|^3-3|p|^2/|p|^5=0$. So $\Phi$ is closed. On the unit sphere, the sphere example of [[differential-forms]] gives $\int_{S_1}(x\,dy\wedge dz+\cdots)=4\pi$, and the denominator is $1$ there, so $\int_{S_1}\Phi=4\pi$.

For general $R$, the region $A$ between $S_1$ and $S_R$ is a compact manifold with boundary $\partial A=S_R-S_1$ (outer sphere with the outward orientation, inner one with the opposite orientation). Stokes gives $\int_{S_R}\Phi-\int_{S_1}\Phi=\int_Ad\Phi=0$. This is exactly the mechanism by which charges in field theory are topological: Bhardwaj et al. define a charge as the integral of a closed form over a cycle and observe that deforming the cycle does not change it, by Stokes. The restriction of $\Phi$ to $S_1$ is the area form, so this example also exhibits a volume form on $S^2$ representing a nonzero class in $H^2(S^2)$.

blocks.body:
1. Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to M$ be a smooth path, viewed as a $1$-simplex, and $f$ a function. Check that $\int_\sigma df=f(\sigma(1))-f(\sigma(0))$ is the chain version of Stokes, with $\partial\sigma=\sigma(1)-\sigma(0)$.
2. On $T^2$, compute the periods of $a\,d\theta_1+b\,d\theta_2$ over the two circles $S^1\times\{1\}$ and $\{1\}\times S^1$, and deduce that $[d\theta_1],[d\theta_2]$ are linearly independent in $H^1(T^2)$.
3. Show that on a compact oriented manifold $M$ without boundary, if $\alpha$ is closed of degree $k$ and $\beta$ is exact of degree $n-k$, then $\int_M\alpha\wedge\beta=0$. Deduce that $\int_M\alpha\wedge\beta$ is a well-defined pairing $H^k(M)\times H^{n-k}(M)\to\mathbb{R}$.
4. Is the area form of $S^2$, restricted to $S^2$ minus a point, exact there? (Use that $S^2$ minus a point is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the Poincaré lemma below.)

blocks.title: Interior product, Lie derivative and Cartan's formula
blocks.body:
Homotopy operators, flows and (on a later page) equivariant cohomology are written with two more operations on forms. For a vector field $X$, the interior product $\iota_X:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k-1}(M)$ inserts $X$ in the first slot:
$$(\iota_X\omega)(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})=\omega(X,v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}),\qquad \iota_Xf=0\ \text{for functions}.$$
It is $C^\infty$-linear in $X$ and in $\omega$, satisfies $\iota_X\iota_Y=-\iota_Y\iota_X$ (so $\iota_X\iota_X=0$), and is an antiderivation of degree $-1$: $\iota_X(\alpha\wedge\beta)=\iota_X\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge\iota_X\beta$ for $\alpha\in\Omega^k$. In coordinates, $$\iota_X(dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k})=\sum_p(-1)^{p-1}X^{i_p}\,dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx_{i_p}}\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k}$$, and $\iota_X(df)=Xf$. Gualtieri introduces $\iota_X$ by exactly these two rules (a graded derivation with $\iota_Xf=0$ and $\iota_Xdf=X(f)$).

If $\varphi_t$ is the (local) flow of $X$, the Lie derivative of a form is
$$L_X\omega=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\varphi_t^*\omega .$$
It preserves degree, is a derivation ($L_X(\alpha\wedge\beta)=L_X\alpha\wedge\beta+\alpha\wedge L_X\beta$, by differentiating $\varphi_t^*(\alpha\wedge\beta)=\varphi_t^*\alpha\wedge\varphi_t^*\beta$), commutes with $d$ (because each $\varphi_t^*$ does), and on functions $L_Xf=Xf$. A remark for readers of Notman–Sanabani: their Theorem 2.45(iii) lists $\iota_X\circ\iota_Y=[X,Y]$; that cannot be right as written, since the left side is antisymmetric under $X\leftrightarrow Y$ and vanishes for $X=Y$. What their later computations need is the anticommutation $\iota_X\iota_Y=-\iota_Y\iota_X$, and the correct commutator rule is $L_X\iota_Y-\iota_YL_X=\iota_{[X,Y]}$.

blocks.title: Cartan's formula
blocks.body:
For every vector field $X$ on $M$,
$$L_X=\iota_X\circ d+d\circ\iota_X\quad\text{on }\Omega^*(M).$$
Consequently, if $\omega$ is closed then $L_X\omega=d(\iota_X\omega)$ is exact, so the flow of $X$ acts trivially on de Rham cohomology to first order.

Let $P=\iota_Xd+d\iota_X$. Three properties of $P$: (i) it is a derivation of degree $0$, because for $\alpha\in\Omega^k$,
$$P(\alpha\wedge\beta)=\iota_X\big(d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta\big)+d\big(\iota_X\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge\iota_X\beta\big),$$
and expanding with the two antiderivation rules, the four cross terms $\pm d\alpha\wedge\iota_X\beta$ and $\pm\iota_X\alpha\wedge d\beta$ cancel in pairs, leaving $P\alpha\wedge\beta+\alpha\wedge P\beta$; (ii) $Pd=\iota_Xdd+d\iota_Xd=d\iota_Xd=dP$; (iii) on functions $Pf=\iota_Xdf=Xf$. The operator $L_X$ has the same three properties. Both operators are local (the value on $\omega$ near $p$ depends only on $\omega$ near $p$), so it suffices to compare them on a chart, where every form is a sum of terms $f\,dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k}$. A degree-$0$ derivation commuting with $d$ is determined by its values on functions: it sends $dx_i$ to $d(Xx_i)$ and then the product rule fixes everything. Since $L_X$ and $P$ agree on functions, they agree on all forms. If $d\omega=0$ the formula reads $L_X\omega=d\iota_X\omega$.

blocks.title: Checking Cartan's formula for a rotation
blocks.body: Let $X=-y\,\partial_x+x\,\partial_y$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose flow is rotation by angle $t$ about the $z$-axis, and $\omega=\alpha+\beta$ with $\alpha=xz\,dy$ and $\beta=y^2\,dx\wedge dz$. Compute $L_X\omega$ from the flow and from Cartan's formula.
blocks.solution:
Flow. $\varphi_t(x,y,z)=(x\cos t-y\sin t,\ x\sin t+y\cos t,\ z)$, so
$$\varphi_t^*\alpha=(x\cos t-y\sin t)\,z\,(\sin t\,dx+\cos t\,dy),\qquad \varphi_t^*\beta=(x\sin t+y\cos t)^2(\cos t\,dx-\sin t\,dy)\wedge dz .$$
Differentiating at $t=0$ gives $L_X\alpha=xz\,dx-yz\,dy$ and $L_X\beta=2xy\,dx\wedge dz-y^2\,dy\wedge dz$.

Cartan, one degree at a time. The useful contractions are $\iota_Xdx=-y$, $\iota_Xdy=x$, $\iota_Xdz=0$, hence $\iota_X(dx\wedge dy)=-y\,dy-x\,dx$, $\iota_X(dx\wedge dz)=-y\,dz$, $\iota_X(dy\wedge dz)=x\,dz$, and $\iota_X(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)=-y\,dy\wedge dz-x\,dx\wedge dz$.

For $\alpha$: $\iota_X\alpha=x^2z$, so $d\iota_X\alpha=2xz\,dx+x^2\,dz$; and $d\alpha=z\,dx\wedge dy-x\,dy\wedge dz$, so $\iota_Xd\alpha=-xz\,dx-yz\,dy-x^2\,dz$. The sum is $xz\,dx-yz\,dy$.

For $\beta$: $\iota_X\beta=-y^3\,dz$, so $d\iota_X\beta=-3y^2\,dy\wedge dz$; and $d\beta=2y\,dy\wedge dx\wedge dz=-2y\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, so $\iota_Xd\beta=2y^2\,dy\wedge dz+2xy\,dx\wedge dz$. The sum is $2xy\,dx\wedge dz-y^2\,dy\wedge dz$.

Both agree with the flow computation. Each of $d\iota_X$ and $\iota_Xd$ maps $k$-forms to $k$-forms on its own; neither half alone equals $L_X$, and only the sum does, which is why it pays to compute the two halves separately and add.

blocks.body:
1. Prove $\iota_X\iota_Y=-\iota_Y\iota_X$ from the definition of $\iota$ as insertion into the first slot.
2. For the Euler field $E=x\,\partial_x+y\,\partial_y+z\,\partial_z$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, show that $L_E(dx_I)=k\,dx_I$ for $|I|=k$ and compute $L_E(f\,dx_I)$ for a homogeneous polynomial $f$ of degree $m$.
3. Use Cartan's formula to show $L_X\iota_X=\iota_XL_X$ and $L_X(\iota_X\omega)=\iota_X(L_X\omega)$.
4. Let $\mu=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. Show that $L_X\mu=(\operatorname{div}X)\,\mu$. Interpret: the flow of $X$ preserves volume exactly when $\operatorname{div}X=0$.

blocks.title: Homotopy invariance and the Poincaré lemma
blocks.body:
The single most useful property of de Rham cohomology is that it does not see smooth deformations. The proof is a formula: an explicit operator $h$ that lowers degree by one and measures the difference between the two ends of a cylinder. Guzmán–Hirani–Liu–Potu quote it from Lee (Lemma 17.9 and Proposition 17.10 of the second edition) as the starting point of their discrete constructions, and Gualtieri proves the same identity by splitting forms on $M\times[0,1]$ into two types.

Setup. Let $I=[0,1]$ and, for $t\in I$, let $i_t:M\to M\times I$ be $i_t(p)=(p,t)$. (Forms on $M\times I$ are smooth up to the boundary; nothing changes if one uses $M\times\mathbb{R}$ instead.) Let $S=\partial/\partial t$, the vector field on $M\times I$ along the interval factor. Define
$$\begin{aligned}h&:\Omega^k(M\times I)\to\Omega^{k-1}(M),\\ h\omega&=\int_0^1 i_t^*\big(\iota_S\,\omega\big)\,dt,\end{aligned}$$
where the integral of a $t$-dependent form on $M$ is taken coefficient by coefficient in any chart.

blocks.title: Homotopy formula
blocks.body:
For every $\omega\in\Omega^k(M\times I)$,
$$d\,h\omega+h\,d\omega=i_1^*\omega-i_0^*\omega .$$
Consequently, if $F,G:M\to N$ are smoothly homotopic via $H:M\times I\to N$ with $H\circ i_0=F$ and $H\circ i_1=G$, then $K=h\circ H^*:\Omega^k(N)\to\Omega^{k-1}(M)$ satisfies $dK+Kd=G^*-F^*$, and therefore $F^*=G^*:H^*(N)\to H^*(M)$.

Every form on $M\times I$ can be written uniquely as
$$\omega=\alpha_t+dt\wedge\beta_t,$$
where $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are forms on $M\times I$ with no $dt$ in them, that is, $t$-dependent forms on $M$ of degrees $k$ and $k-1$. (In a chart $(x,t)$, collect the terms containing $dt$ and move $dt$ to the front.) Then $i_t^*\omega=\alpha_t$, because $i_t^*dt=0$. Since $\iota_S\,dt=1$ and $\iota_S$ kills every $dx_j$, the antiderivation rule gives $\iota_S\omega=\beta_t$. So $h\omega=\int_0^1\beta_t\,dt$.

Now compute $d\omega$. Split $d=d_M+dt\wedge\partial_t$, where $d_M$ differentiates only in the $M$ directions. Then
$$d\omega=d_M\alpha_t+dt\wedge\partial_t\alpha_t-dt\wedge d_M\beta_t,$$
using $d(dt\wedge\beta_t)=-dt\wedge d\beta_t$ and $dt\wedge dt=0$. The part containing $dt$ is $dt\wedge(\partial_t\alpha_t-d_M\beta_t)$, so
$$h\,d\omega=\int_0^1\big(\partial_t\alpha_t-d_M\beta_t\big)\,dt=\alpha_1-\alpha_0-d_M\!\int_0^1\beta_t\,dt=i_1^*\omega-i_0^*\omega-d\,h\omega,$$
where we used the fundamental theorem of calculus coefficientwise and the fact that $d_M$ commutes with integration in $t$ (differentiation under the integral sign, legitimate for smooth integrands on a compact interval). This is the formula.

For the consequence, apply the formula to $H^*\omega$ and use $i_t^*H^*=(H\circ i_t)^*$ and $dH^*=H^*d$: $$dK\omega+Kd\omega=dhH^*\omega+hdH^*\omega=i_1^*H^*\omega-i_0^*H^*\omega=G^*\omega-F^*\omega$$. If $\omega$ is closed, $G^*\omega-F^*\omega=d(K\omega)$ is exact, so $F^*[\omega]=G^*[\omega]$.

blocks.title: Homotopy invariance and the Poincaré lemma
blocks.body:
1. If $F:M\to N$ is a smooth homotopy equivalence (there is $G:N\to M$ with $G\circ F$ and $F\circ G$ smoothly homotopic to the identities), then $F^*:H^*(N)\to H^*(M)$ is a ring isomorphism. In particular a deformation retract has the same cohomology as the whole space.
2. (Poincaré lemma.) If $M$ is smoothly contractible, for example a star-shaped open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, then $H^0(M)=\mathbb{R}$ and $H^k(M)=0$ for $k\ge1$. So every closed $k$-form with $k\ge1$ on such a set is exact.

1. $F^*G^*=(G\circ F)^*=\mathrm{id}^*=\mathrm{id}$ on $H^*(M)$ and $G^*F^*=\mathrm{id}$ on $H^*(N)$ by the homotopy formula, so $F^*$ is bijective; it is a ring map by functoriality. A deformation retraction $r:M\to A$ onto a submanifold $A$ is a homotopy inverse of the inclusion.

2. A smooth contraction is a homotopy between $\mathrm{id}_M$ and a constant map $c$. The constant map factors through a point, whose cohomology is $\mathbb{R}$ in degree $0$ and $0$ otherwise. So $\mathrm{id}=c^*$ is zero on $H^k$ for $k\ge1$, and $H^0=\mathbb{R}$ because $M$ is connected. A star-shaped set (with respect to $0$, say) is contracted by $H(x,t)=tx$.

Gualtieri adds that a continuous homotopy between smooth maps can be replaced by a smooth one, so de Rham cohomology is in fact invariant under continuous homotopy equivalence; we only use the smooth version.

blocks.title: Why deformations do not change cohomology

items.label: Integrate along the cylinder
items.body: Gualtieri and Guzmán–Hirani–Liu–Potu (quoting Lee) write down one operator $h$ on $M\times[0,1]$ that integrates the $dt$-component of a form over the interval; the identity $dh+hd=i_1^*-i_0^*$ is the fundamental theorem of calculus in $t$, and it shows at once that the two ends of a homotopy induce the same map.

items.label: Products with a line
items.body: Bott–Tu first prove that $\pi^*:H^*(\mathbb{R}^n)\to H^*(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R})$ is an isomorphism with inverse $s^*$, for any manifold in place of $\mathbb{R}^n$, using their operator $K$; the homotopy axiom follows because a homotopy factors through $M\times\mathbb{R}$, on which the two inclusions $s_0,s_1$ are both inverse to $\pi^*$.

items.label: Flows, infinitesimally
items.body: For a vector field $X$ with flow $\varphi_t$, Cartan's formula gives $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi_t^*\omega=\varphi_t^*L_X\omega=d\big(\varphi_t^*\iota_X\omega\big)$ for closed $\omega$, so the class of $\varphi_t^*\omega$ is constant in $t$. Notman–Sanabani use Cartan's formula in the same way to show that the Cartan differential squares to zero on invariant forms.

items.label: Contractions on cochains
items.body: On a simplicial complex the same idea becomes a cone operator on chains, $\mathrm{Co}\,\partial+\partial\,\mathrm{Co}=\mathrm{id}$; its dual on cochains is a discrete Poincaré operator, and its existence certifies that cohomology vanishes in positive degrees without computing any ranks.

blocks.title: The Poincaré operator on a star-shaped domain
blocks.body: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be star-shaped with respect to $0$. Derive from the homotopy formula an explicit operator $K$ with $dK\omega+Kd\omega=\omega$ for every $k$-form, $k\ge1$, and use it (a) to find a potential of the closed $1$-form $\omega=(2xy+z)\,dx+x^2\,dy+(x+3z^2)\,dz$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and (b) to write a vector potential for a divergence-free field $B$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
blocks.solution:
Use $H(x,t)=tx$, so $H\circ i_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $H\circ i_0$ is constant. A constant map pulls back every form of positive degree to $0$, so $K=h\circ H^*$ satisfies $dK+Kd=\mathrm{id}$ on $k$-forms, $k\ge1$. To compute $K$, note $H^*(dx_i)=t\,dx_i+x_i\,dt$. Hence $H^*(f\,dx_I)=f(tx)\bigwedge_{i\in I}(t\,dx_i+x_i\,dt)$; only the terms with exactly one $dt$ survive $\iota_S$, and moving that $dt$ to the front gives
$$K\omega(x)=\int_0^1 t^{k-1}\,\iota_E\big(\omega(tx)\big)\,dt,\qquad E=\sum_i x_i\,\partial_i,$$
where $\omega(tx)$ means the form with coefficients evaluated at $tx$ and the contraction with the Euler field $E$ uses the unscaled $x$. This is the cone (Poincaré) operator that the discrete constructions of Guzmán–Hirani–Liu–Potu imitate on simplicial complexes.

(a) $d\omega=0$ (check $\partial_yP=\partial_xQ=2x$, $\partial_zP=\partial_xR=1$, $\partial_zQ=\partial_yR=0$), so $\omega=d(K\omega)$ with $K\omega(x,y,z)=\int_0^1\big(x(2t^2xy+tz)+y\,t^2x^2+z(tx+3t^2z^2)\big)dt=x^2y+xz+z^3$. Indeed $d(x^2y+xz+z^3)=(2xy+z)\,dx+x^2\,dy+(x+3z^2)\,dz$.

(b) Encode $B$ as the $2$-form $\beta=B_1\,dy\wedge dz+B_2\,dz\wedge dx+B_3\,dx\wedge dy$; then $d\beta=(\operatorname{div}B)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=0$. One computes $\iota_E\beta=(B\times x)_1dx+(B\times x)_2dy+(B\times x)_3dz$, so $K\beta$ is the $1$-form of the vector field
$$A(x)=\int_0^1 t\,B(tx)\times x\,dt,$$
and $dK\beta=\beta$ says $\operatorname{curl}A=B$. For constant $B=(0,0,1)$ this gives $A=\tfrac12(-y,x,0)$. The same operator applied to a non-closed form returns $\omega-Kd\omega$, not $\omega$; closedness is what makes the correction term vanish.

blocks.title: Signs in homotopy operators
blocks.body: The homotopy formula appears in three shapes in the sources, differing in where $dt$ is placed and over which interval one integrates. All give the same cohomological conclusion; the signs matter when a paper manipulates the operators themselves.

rows.text: $h\omega=\int_0^1i_t^*(\iota_{\partial_t}\omega)\,dt$ on $M\times I$, with $dh+hd=i_1^*-i_0^*$ and no sign. For a homotopy $\Phi$ from $F$ to $G$, $K=h\circ\Phi^*$ gives $dK+Kd=G^*-F^*$.
$K$ kills forms without $dt$ and sends $f\,dt\wedge\beta\mapsto(\int_0^1f\,dt)\,\beta$, with $J_1^*-J_0^*=dK+Kd$; the same operator as above, written with $dt$ in front.

On $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$, $K$ kills forms without $dt$ and sends $(\pi^*\varphi)f(x,t)\,dt\mapsto(\pi^*\varphi)\int_0^tf(x,u)\,du$, with $dt$ written on the right. The identity becomes $1-\pi^*s^*=(-1)^{q-1}(dK-Kd)$ on $q$-forms, where $s(x)=(x,0)$ and $\pi$ is the projection.

blocks.body:
- Simply connected is not enough. Simple connectivity forces $H^1=0$ (a closed $1$-form integrates to zero over every loop, since loops are null-homotopic, so it has a potential), but says nothing about $H^2$: $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$ is simply connected and $H^2(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\})=\mathbb{R}$. The Poincaré lemma needs contractibility (or star-shapedness). The Wikipedia summary of the Poincaré lemma groups "contractible" and "simply connected" together in one sentence; only the first is correct in all degrees.
- The Poincaré operator is not a projection onto potentials of arbitrary forms. $K\omega$ is a potential only when $d\omega=0$; in general $dK\omega=\omega-Kd\omega$.
- A closed form being exact on every ball does not make it exact. The angle form is exact on every slit plane but not on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$; local exactness is automatic, and cohomology is the obstruction to patching the local potentials.
- Homotopy invariance concerns maps, not forms: two cohomologous forms need not be related by any diffeomorphism, and two forms pulled back by homotopic maps are equal only as classes.

1. Use homotopy invariance to show $H^*(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})\cong H^*(S^{n-1})$ and that the Möbius band has the cohomology of the circle.
2. Compute $K\omega$ for $\omega=dx\wedge dy$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and verify $dK\omega=\omega$.
3. Let $B=(yz,x^2,xy)$. Check $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and compute the vector potential $A(x)=\int_0^1tB(tx)\times x\,dt$; verify $\operatorname{curl}A=B$.
4. Verify Bott–Tu's identity $1-\pi^*s^*=(-1)^{q-1}(dK-Kd)$ by hand on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$ for a $1$-form $f(x,t)\,dx$ and for a $1$-form $g(x,t)\,dt$.
5. Show that if $F:M\to N$ is smoothly homotopic to a constant map then $F^*=0$ on $H^k(N)$ for all $k\ge1$. Deduce that the identity of $S^n$ is not homotopic to a constant map (use the next section's $H^n(S^n)=\mathbb{R}$).

blocks.title: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence
blocks.body:
Homotopy invariance computes contractible pieces; the Mayer–Vietoris sequence glues pieces together. It is the main computational tool of Bott–Tu, who use it to prove almost every structural theorem of their first chapter, and it is the de Rham counterpart of the Mayer–Vietoris sequence in [[homology]]. It comes from a short exact sequence of complexes, so we first record the algebra that turns short exact sequences of complexes into long exact sequences.

A cochain complex is a sequence of vector spaces $A^k$ with maps $d:A^k\to A^{k+1}$, $d^2=0$, and $H^k(A)=\ker d/\operatorname{im}d$. A cochain map $f:A\to B$ commutes with $d$ and induces $f^*:H^k(A)\to H^k(B)$. A sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to0$ of cochain maps is short exact if in each degree $f$ is injective, $g$ is surjective and $\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$.

blocks.title: Long exact sequence of a short exact sequence of complexes
blocks.body:
A short exact sequence of cochain complexes $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to0$ induces a long exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}\cdots\to H^k(A)&\xrightarrow{f^*}H^k(B)\xrightarrow{g^*}H^k(C)\\&\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{k+1}(A)\xrightarrow{f^*}H^{k+1}(B)\to\cdots\end{aligned}$$
where the connecting map is $\delta[c]=[a]$ for any $a$ with $f(a)=d b$ and $g(b)=c$.

Definition of $\delta$. Let $c\in C^k$ be closed. Choose $b\in B^k$ with $g(b)=c$ ($g$ is onto). Then $g(db)=dg(b)=dc=0$, so $db=f(a)$ for a unique $a\in A^{k+1}$ ($\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$, $f$ injective). And $f(da)=d f(a)=ddb=0$, so $da=0$. If $b$ is replaced by $b+f(a')$ (the only freedom), $a$ changes by $da'$; if $c$ is replaced by $c+dc'$, write $c'=g(b')$ and replace $b$ by $b+db'$, which does not change $db$. So $[a]$ depends only on $[c]$. Linearity is clear.

Exactness at $H^k(B)$: $g^*f^*=(gf)^*=0$. If $g(b)=dc'$ with $b$ closed, write $c'=g(b')$; then $g(b-db')=0$, so $b-db'=f(a)$ with $f(da)=d(b-db')=0$, hence $a$ closed and $[b]=f^*[a]$.

Exactness at $H^k(C)$: $\delta g^*[b]$ is computed with the lift $b$ itself, $db=0$, so $a=0$. Conversely if $\delta[c]=0$, then $a=da''$ and $b-f(a'')$ is closed with $g(b-f(a''))=c$.

Exactness at $H^{k+1}(A)$: $f^*\delta[c]=[f(a)]=[db]=0$. Conversely if $f(a)=db$ with $a$ closed, then $c=g(b)$ is closed ($dc=g(db)=gf(a)=0$) and $\delta[c]=[a]$ by construction.

blocks.title: Mayer–Vietoris sequence
blocks.body:
Let $M=U\cup V$ with $U,V$ open. With the restriction maps, the sequence
$$\begin{gathered}0\to\Omega^*(M)\xrightarrow{\ r\ }\Omega^*(U)\oplus\Omega^*(V)\xrightarrow{\ s\ }\Omega^*(U\cap V)\to0,\\ r(\omega)=(\omega|_U,\omega|_V),\qquad s(\alpha,\beta)=\beta|_{U\cap V}-\alpha|_{U\cap V},\end{gathered}$$
is a short exact sequence of complexes. Hence there is a long exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^k(M)\to H^k(U)\oplus H^k(V)\to H^k(U\cap V)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{k+1}(M)\to\cdots$$
If $\{\rho_U,\rho_V\}$ is a partition of unity subordinate to $\{U,V\}$ and $\omega$ is a closed form on $U\cap V$, then $\delta[\omega]$ is represented by the global form equal to $-d(\rho_V\omega)$ on $U$ and to $d(\rho_U\omega)$ on $V$. (Here $\rho_V\omega$, defined on $U\cap V$, is extended by zero to $U$, and similarly for $\rho_U\omega$.)

Restriction commutes with $d$, so $r$ and $s$ are cochain maps. $r$ is injective: a form vanishing on $U$ and on $V$ vanishes on $M$. $s\circ r=0$ clearly, and if $s(\alpha,\beta)=0$ then $\alpha$ and $\beta$ agree on $U\cap V$ and glue to a form on $M$, so $\ker s=\operatorname{im}r$.

Surjectivity of $s$ is where the partition of unity enters. Given $\omega\in\Omega^k(U\cap V)$, the form $\rho_V\omega$ on $U\cap V$ extends by zero to a smooth form on $U$: its support is contained in $\operatorname{supp}\rho_V$, which is closed in $M$, and $U\cap\operatorname{supp}\rho_V$ is closed in $U$ and lies in $U\cap V$, so near any point of $U\setminus V$ the extension is zero. Similarly $\rho_U\omega$ extends by zero to $V$. Then
$$s(-\rho_V\omega,\ \rho_U\omega)=\rho_U\omega+\rho_V\omega=\omega\quad\text{on }U\cap V .$$
So the sequence is short exact and the previous theorem applies. The recipe for $\delta$ is the definition of the connecting map with the lift $b=(-\rho_V\omega,\rho_U\omega)$: $db=(-d(\rho_V\omega),d(\rho_U\omega))$, and on $U\cap V$ the two components agree, since $d(\rho_U\omega)+d(\rho_V\omega)=d\omega=0$; so $db=r(a)$ for the global form $a$ described.

blocks.alt: Top row: zero, Omega of M, Omega of U plus Omega of V, Omega of U intersect V, zero, joined by arrows r and s. Below, the long exact sequence H^k(M) to H^k(U) plus H^k(V) to H^k(U cap V), with a diagonal arrow delta going down to H^{k+1}(M) on the next row.

blocks.title: The circle by Mayer–Vietoris, with an explicit generator
blocks.body: Cover $S^1$ by $U=S^1\setminus\{N\}$ and $V=S^1\setminus\{S\}$, where $N$ and $S$ are the points at angles $\pi/2$ and $-\pi/2$. Compute $H^*(S^1)$ from the Mayer–Vietoris sequence, and find a generator of $H^1(S^1)$ as $\delta$ of a function on $U\cap V$, computing its integral.
blocks.solution:
$U$ and $V$ are open arcs, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$, and $U\cap V=A\sqcup B$ with $A$ the open right half-circle and $B$ the open left half-circle. So $H^0(U)=H^0(V)=\mathbb{R}$, $H^0(U\cap V)=\mathbb{R}^2$, and all $H^1$ of the pieces vanish. The sequence is
$$0\to H^0(S^1)\to\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathbb{R}\xrightarrow{s}\mathbb{R}^2\xrightarrow{\delta}H^1(S^1)\to0 .$$
The map $s$ sends constants $(a,b)$ to the function equal to $b-a$ on both $A$ and $B$, so its image is the line of functions that are equal constants on $A$ and $B$. Hence $H^0(S^1)=\ker s=\mathbb{R}$ and $H^1(S^1)\cong\mathbb{R}^2/\operatorname{im}s\cong\mathbb{R}$. (Petrov reaches the same dimension count by noting that the alternating sum of dimensions in an exact sequence of finite-dimensional spaces is zero.)

A generator is $\delta[\alpha]$ for $\alpha$ equal to $1$ on $A$ and $0$ on $B$, since $\alpha\notin\operatorname{im}s$. By the recipe, $\delta\alpha$ is $d(\rho_U\alpha)$ on $V$ and $-d(\rho_V\alpha)$ on $U$; both vanish outside $A$, and on $A$ the form is $d\rho_U$. The function $\rho_U$ is $1$ near $S$ (where $\rho_V=0$) and $0$ near $N$. Integrating counterclockwise across $A$, from just after $S$ to just before $N$,
$$\int_{S^1}\delta\alpha=\int_A d\rho_U=\rho_U(\text{near }N)-\rho_U(\text{near }S)=0-1=-1 .$$
So $\delta\alpha$ is a bump $1$-form supported in $A$ with total integral $-1$, cohomologous to $-\frac{1}{2\pi}d\theta$. Bott–Tu construct the generator of $H^1(S^1)$ in this way; with the opposite sign convention for $s$ the integral would be $+1$.

blocks.caption: The cover of $S^1$ by $U=S^1\setminus\{N\}$ (blue, inside) and $V=S^1\setminus\{S\}$ (red, outside). Their intersection has two components $A$ and $B$; the generator $\delta\alpha$ of $H^1(S^1)$ is supported in $A$.
blocks.alt: A circle with the north point N and south point S marked. A blue arc drawn just inside the circle covers everything except N; a red arc just outside covers everything except S. The right half-circle is labelled A and the left half-circle B.

blocks.title: Cohomology of spheres
blocks.body: For $n\ge1$, $H^k(S^n)\cong\mathbb{R}$ for $k=0$ and $k=n$, and $H^k(S^n)=0$ otherwise. A generator of $H^n(S^n)$ is the class of any $n$-form with nonzero integral, for instance the area form.

Induction on $n$, the case $n=1$ being the example above. For $n\ge2$ cover $S^n$ by $U=S^n\setminus\{N\}$ and $V=S^n\setminus\{S\}$; both are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ by stereographic projection, and $U\cap V\cong\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ deformation retracts onto $S^{n-1}$. For $k\ge1$ the outer terms $H^k(U)\oplus H^k(V)$ and $H^{k+1}(U)\oplus H^{k+1}(V)$ vanish by the Poincaré lemma, so $\delta:H^k(U\cap V)\to H^{k+1}(S^n)$ is an isomorphism: $H^{k+1}(S^n)\cong H^k(S^{n-1})$ for $k\ge1$. In degrees $0$ and $1$: $U\cap V$ is connected (as $n\ge2$), so $H^0(U)\oplus H^0(V)\to H^0(U\cap V)$, $(a,b)\mapsto b-a$, is onto; exactness then gives $H^0(S^n)=\mathbb{R}$ and $H^1(S^n)=0$. Combining, $H^k(S^n)\cong H^{k-1}(S^{n-1})$ for $k\ge2$, and the induction hypothesis gives the answer. The last sentence follows from the theorem on top-degree classes: integration is a nonzero linear map $H^n(S^n)\to\mathbb{R}$ on a one-dimensional space.

blocks.title: The plane with several punctures
blocks.body: Show that $H^1(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{p_1,\dots,p_m\})\cong\mathbb{R}^m$ for distinct points $p_j$, with basis the classes of the angle forms $\omega_{p_j}$, and $H^2=0$.
blocks.solution:
Induction on $m$. For $m=0$ use the Poincaré lemma; for $m=1$ homotopy invariance gives $H^*(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{p\})\cong H^*(S^1)$. After a rotation and translation we may assume that the $p_j$ have distinct $x$-coordinates and that a vertical line $x=c$ separates $p_1,\dots,p_{m-1}$ (on the left) from $p_m$. Let $U=\{x< c+\epsilon\}\setminus\{p_1,\dots,p_{m-1}\}$ and $V=\{x>c-\epsilon\}\setminus\{p_m\}$ with $\epsilon$ small; then $U\cap V$ is a strip, contractible, and $U\cup V$ is the $m$-punctured plane. By induction (a half-plane is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$), $H^1(U)=\mathbb{R}^{m-1}$, $H^1(V)=\mathbb{R}$, and $H^2$ of both vanish. In the sequence
$$H^0(U)\oplus H^0(V)\to H^0(U\cap V)\to H^1(U\cup V)\to H^1(U)\oplus H^1(V)\to H^1(U\cap V)=0$$
the first map is onto (constants), so $\delta=0$ on $H^0$ and $H^1(U\cup V)\cong H^1(U)\oplus H^1(V)=\mathbb{R}^m$; also $H^2(U\cup V)$ sits between $H^1(U\cap V)=0$ and $H^2(U)\oplus H^2(V)=0$. The restrictions of $\omega_{p_1},\dots,\omega_{p_m}$ to $U$ and $V$ give the bases by induction, and the period computation of the two-puncture example shows directly that they are independent.

blocks.title: Signs in Mayer–Vietoris and in boundary orientations
blocks.body: Changing a sign convention here changes connecting maps by a sign and never changes exactness; it matters when a paper writes an explicit generator or a commuting diagram.

rows.text: Difference map $(\omega,\tau)\mapsto\tau-\omega$ in Example 2.6, lift $(-\rho_V\omega,\rho_U\omega)$, so $\delta[\omega]$ is $-d(\rho_V\omega)$ on $U$ and $d(\rho_U\omega)$ on $V$. This page follows this convention.

$j(\omega,\eta)=\omega|_{U\cap V}-\eta|_{U\cap V}$, the opposite order, with the corresponding lift $(g\sigma,-f\sigma)$ for a partition of unity $f+g=1$; with this lift the explicit formula for the connecting map changes sign (Petrov himself describes $\delta$ only in words and refers to Lee for the formula).
Difference of restrictions, with $\delta[\omega]=[\eta]$ where $\eta=-d(\rho_V\omega)=d(\rho_U\omega)$, matching Bott–Tu.

For the upper half-space $\{x_n\ge0\}$ the boundary $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ is oriented by $(-1)^n\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{n-1}$, chosen so that Stokes has no sign. This is the outward-normal-first rule of [[differential-forms]] and of Gualtieri written in coordinates: the outward normal is $-\partial_n$, and $\det(-e_n,e_1,\dots,e_{n-1})=(-1)^n$.

blocks.title: Good covers and finite dimensionality
blocks.body:
Mayer–Vietoris arguments run by induction on the number of open sets in a cover whose pieces and intersections are as simple as possible. An open cover $\{U_\alpha\}$ of an $n$-manifold is good if every nonempty finite intersection $U_{\alpha_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{\alpha_p}$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$. Guillemin–Haine use the closely related notion of finite topology: a finite cover all of whose nonempty intersections are diffeomorphic to convex open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a convex open set is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$, so this is a finite good cover).

Every manifold has a good cover, and a compact manifold has a finite one (Bott–Tu, §5; Guillemin–Haine, Appendix C). The proof chooses a Riemannian metric and takes small geodesically convex balls: an intersection of geodesically convex sets is geodesically convex, and such a set is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$. We use this fact without proof; for open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ one can see it directly with Euclidean balls, which are convex.

blocks.title: Finite good covers give finite-dimensional cohomology
blocks.body: If $M$ has a finite good cover then $H^k(M)$ is finite dimensional for every $k$. In particular this holds for compact manifolds.

Induction on the number $p$ of open sets in a good cover. If $p=1$, $M\cong\mathbb{R}^n$ and the Poincaré lemma applies. Suppose the claim holds for all manifolds with good covers of at most $p$ sets, and let $U_1,\dots,U_{p+1}$ be a good cover of $M$. Put $U=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_p$ and $V=U_{p+1}$. Then $U$ has the good cover $U_1,\dots,U_p$, $V\cong\mathbb{R}^n$, and $U\cap V$ has the good cover $U_1\cap U_{p+1},\dots,U_p\cap U_{p+1}$ (intersections of these are intersections of the original sets). In the exact sequence
$$H^{k-1}(U\cap V)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^k(M)\xrightarrow{r}H^k(U)\oplus H^k(V)$$
the image of $r$ is finite dimensional and $\ker r=\operatorname{im}\delta$ is finite dimensional, so $H^k(M)$ is.

blocks.title: Euler characteristic from a good cover
blocks.body: For $M$ with a finite good cover, define $\chi(M)=\sum_k(-1)^k\dim H^k(M)$. Show that $\chi(U\cup V)=\chi(U)+\chi(V)-\chi(U\cap V)$ when all four have finite good covers, and compute $\chi(S^n)$ and $\chi$ of the plane with $m$ punctures.
blocks.solution: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence is a finite exact sequence of finite-dimensional spaces (it stops at degree $n$), so the alternating sum of the dimensions of its terms vanishes. Grouping the terms by type, $\chi(M)-\big(\chi(U)+\chi(V)\big)+\chi(U\cap V)=0$. For spheres, the theorem above gives $\chi(S^n)=1+(-1)^n$, so $2$ for even $n$ and $0$ for odd $n$; inclusion–exclusion with two discs meeting in an annulus agrees: $1+1-\chi(S^{n-1})$. For the plane with $m$ punctures, $\chi=1-m$. These match the simplicial Euler characteristics of [[homology]], as de Rham's theorem predicts.

blocks.title: The Künneth formula and tori
blocks.body:
Products are the other basic way to build manifolds. If $\pi:M\times F\to M$ and $\rho:M\times F\to F$ are the projections, the map
$$\psi:\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^p(M)\otimes H^q(F)\to H^k(M\times F),\qquad[\omega]\otimes[\varphi]\mapsto[\pi^*\omega\wedge\rho^*\varphi],$$
is well defined (products and pullbacks of closed forms are closed, and exact factors give exact products). Petrov states the Künneth theorem as $H^*(M\times F)\cong H^*(M)\otimes H^*(F)$ and refers to Bott–Tu for the proof by induction on a good cover, which we now give.

blocks.title: Künneth formula
blocks.body:
If $M$ has a finite good cover, then $\psi$ is an isomorphism for every manifold $F$:
$$H^k(M\times F)\cong\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^p(M)\otimes H^q(F).$$
If both have finite-dimensional cohomology, the Poincaré polynomials $P_X(t)=\sum_kb_k(X)t^k$ multiply: $P_{M\times F}=P_MP_F$.

Fix $F$ and argue by induction on the number of sets in a good cover of $M$. If $M\cong\mathbb{R}^n$, then $M\times F$ deformation retracts to $\{0\}\times F$, $H^*(M)=\mathbb{R}$ in degree $0$, and $\psi$ reduces to $\rho^*:H^*(F)\to H^*(\mathbb{R}^n\times F)$, an isomorphism by homotopy invariance.

For $M=U\cup V$, the Mayer–Vietoris sequence of $M$ tensored with the fixed vector space $H^q(F)$ stays exact (tensoring over a field is exact), and summing over $p+q=k$ gives an exact sequence of the left-hand sides for $U$, $V$, $U\cap V$, $M$. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence of $M\times F=(U\times F)\cup(V\times F)$ gives one for the right-hand sides. The maps $\psi$ commute with restrictions, and with the connecting maps: using the partition of unity $\pi^*\rho_U,\pi^*\rho_V$ on $M\times F$,
$$\delta[\pi^*\omega\wedge\rho^*\varphi]=\big[-d(\pi^*\rho_V\,\pi^*\omega\wedge\rho^*\varphi)\big]=\big[\pi^*(-d(\rho_V\omega))\wedge\rho^*\varphi\big]=\psi(\delta[\omega]\otimes[\varphi])$$
on $U\times F$ (similarly on $V\times F$), since $d\rho^*\varphi=0$. The [[homological-algebra|five lemma]] and the same induction on the number of sets as in the proof of finite dimensionality finish the argument. The statement about Poincaré polynomials is the dimension count of the direct sum of tensor products.

blocks.title: Tori of every dimension
blocks.body: Compute $H^*(T^n)$ for $T^n=S^1\times\cdots\times S^1$, with basis and ring structure, and the Betti numbers of $T^3$.
blocks.solution: $S^1$ is compact, so it has a finite good cover, and by induction Künneth applies to $T^n=T^{n-1}\times S^1$. With $P_{S^1}(t)=1+t$, $P_{T^n}(t)=(1+t)^n$, so $b_k(T^n)=\binom nk$. Unwinding $\psi$, a basis of $H^k(T^n)$ is $[d\theta_I]=[d\theta_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge d\theta_{i_k}]$ for increasing multi-indices $I$, where $\theta_i$ is the angle on the $i$-th factor. The ring is the exterior algebra $\Lambda(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ with $x_i=[d\theta_i]$ in degree $1$; nonvanishing of $x_1\cdots x_n$ is confirmed by $\int_{T^n}d\theta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\theta_n=(2\pi)^n$. For $T^3$: $b=(1,3,3,1)$, $\chi=0$, and [[poincare-duality|Poincaré duality]] is visible as $b_k=b_{3-k}$. Wikipedia describes the same answer: Betti numbers $\binom nk$ and classes represented by wedges of the degree-one forms.

blocks.title: Products of spheres
blocks.body: Compute $H^*(S^2\times S^2)$ with its ring structure, and $H^*(S^1\times S^2)$.
blocks.solution: $P_{S^2\times S^2}=(1+t^2)^2=1+2t^2+t^4$, so $b=(1,0,2,0,1)$ with $H^2$ spanned by $a=[\pi^*\mu_1]$ and $b=[\rho^*\mu_2]$ for normalised area forms $\mu_i$ (integral $1$). Then $a^2=b^2=0$ (pullbacks of $4$-forms on $S^2$) and $ab$ generates $H^4$ with $\int ab=1$. $P_{S^1\times S^2}=(1+t)(1+t^2)=1+t+t^2+t^3$. In the basis $a,b$ the pairing $(x,y)\mapsto\int_{S^2\times S^2}xy$ on $H^2$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, nondegenerate as [[poincare-duality|Poincaré duality]] requires.

blocks.title: De Rham's theorem
blocks.body:
De Rham proved in 1931 that integration identifies the groups on this page with real singular cohomology. To state this we need cohomology on the singular side. For a space $X$, the real singular cochains are $C^k(X;\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}(C_k(X),\mathbb{R})$ with coboundary $(\delta\lambda)(\sigma)=\lambda(\partial\sigma)$, and $H^k(X;\mathbb{R})$ is the cohomology of this complex (Ginory, Definitions 3.1 to 3.3). Because $\mathbb{R}$ is a field, the universal coefficient theorem reduces to
$$H^k(X;\mathbb{R})\cong\operatorname{Hom}\big(H_k(X),\mathbb{R}\big),\qquad[\lambda]\mapsto\big([c]\mapsto\lambda(c)\big),$$
and Chua simply takes the right side as the definition. Singular cohomology inherits from [[homology]] functoriality, homotopy invariance and a Mayer–Vietoris sequence for open covers (dualise the homology sequence; $\operatorname{Hom}(-,\mathbb{R})$ preserves exactness).

To integrate we need smooth chains. Let $H_k^\infty(M)$ be the homology of the smooth chain complex $C^\infty_*(M)$ from the section on integration.

blocks.title: Smooth chains suffice
blocks.body: The inclusion $C^\infty_*(M)\subseteq C_*(M)$ induces isomorphisms $H^\infty_k(M)\cong H_k(M)$ for all $k$. Proof not given here: see Ginory, Theorem 4.4 (each simplex is joined to a smooth one by a homotopy compatible with faces, built inductively with the Whitney approximation theorem, and prism operators give the chain homotopy), or Lee, Chapter 18, cited by Petrov as Theorem 18.7.

blocks.title: The de Rham homomorphism
blocks.body:
For a closed $k$-form $\omega$ define
$$I[\omega]\in H^k(M;\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R}),\qquad I[\omega]\big([c]\big)=\int_{c}\omega,$$
where $c$ is a smooth cycle representing the class (possible by the previous theorem). It is well defined by Stokes, exactly as for periods: exact forms integrate to $0$ on cycles and closed forms integrate to $0$ on boundaries. It is natural, $I\circ F^*=F^*\circ I$ for smooth $F$, because $\int_{F\circ\sigma}\omega=\int_\sigma F^*\omega$.

In words: a de Rham class is turned into the function "integrate over this cycle".

blocks.title: De Rham's theorem
blocks.body: For every smooth manifold $M$ and every $k$, the de Rham homomorphism $I:H^k(M)\to H^k(M;\mathbb{R})$ is an isomorphism. It is natural in $M$, and it carries the wedge product to the cup product, so it is an isomorphism of graded rings. Consequently de Rham cohomology is a topological (indeed homotopy) invariant: homeomorphic manifolds have isomorphic de Rham cohomology rings.

We follow the argument that Petrov and Ginory take from Lee, who credits it to Bredon; Chua outlines the same steps. Call $M$ a de Rham manifold if $I$ is an isomorphism in every degree, and call an open cover a de Rham cover if every finite intersection of its members is a de Rham manifold. The multiplicativity is not proved here; Chua and Wikipedia state it, and it is not needed for the dimension statements used on this page.

Step 0: compatibility with Mayer–Vietoris. For $M=U\cup V$, the integration maps for $U$, $V$, $U\cap V$, $M$ form a map from the de Rham Mayer–Vietoris sequence to the singular one. The squares involving restrictions commute by naturality. The square with the connecting maps commutes too; this is a direct check with the formula for $\delta$ and a decomposition of cycles into $U$-small and $V$-small pieces, done in Petrov, Proposition 5.3(b), and in Lee, Chapter 18. We take it from there.

Step 1: convex open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are de Rham. For $k\ge1$ both sides vanish (Poincaré lemma; contractible spaces have the homology of a point). For $k=0$ both sides are $\mathbb{R}$, and $I$ sends the constant function $1$ to the functional taking the value $1$ on the class of a point, which is nonzero.

Step 2: disjoint unions. If $M=\bigsqcup_jM_j$ with each $M_j$ de Rham, then both sides are products over $j$ (for singular cohomology, $H_k(M)=\bigoplus_jH_k(M_j)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\bigoplus,\mathbb{R})=\prod\operatorname{Hom}$), and $I$ is the product of the $I_j$.

Step 3: finite de Rham covers. If $U$, $V$ and $U\cap V$ are de Rham, the ladder of the two Mayer–Vietoris sequences (the figure below, with $\Phi=I$) and the [[homological-algebra|five lemma]] show that $U\cup V$ is de Rham. By induction on the number of sets, a manifold with a finite de Rham cover is de Rham: for $U_1,\dots,U_{p+1}$, put $U=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_p$ and $V=U_{p+1}$; then $U$ and $U\cap V$ have de Rham covers of $p$ sets.

Step 4: de Rham bases. Suppose $M$ has a de Rham cover that is a basis of its topology. Choose a smooth proper exhaustion function $f:M\to[0,\infty)$ and set $A_m=f^{-1}([m,m+1])$ (compact) and $A'_m=f^{-1}\big((m-\tfrac12,m+\tfrac32)\big)$. Cover $A_m$ by finitely many basis sets inside $A'_m$ and let $B_m$ be their union; it is covered by finitely many basis sets, all of whose finite intersections are de Rham by assumption, so $B_m$ is de Rham by Step 3. Since $B_m\subseteq A'_m$, $B_m$ meets only $B_{m-1}$ and $B_{m+1}$. Let $U=\bigcup_{m\text{ odd}}B_m$ and $V=\bigcup_{m\text{ even}}B_m$. Each is a disjoint union of de Rham manifolds, hence de Rham by Step 2, and $U\cap V=\bigsqcup_m(B_m\cap B_{m+1})$ is a disjoint union of manifolds with finite de Rham covers (by the pairwise intersections of the chosen basis sets), hence de Rham. Step 3 applied to $M=U\cup V$ finishes this step.

Step 5: open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ have the basis of convex balls, and finite intersections of convex sets are convex, so by Steps 1 and 4 they are de Rham. Every manifold has a basis consisting of open sets diffeomorphic to open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (chart domains), whose finite intersections are again of that kind, so Step 4 applies to every manifold.

blocks.caption: The comparison ladder in the proof of de Rham's theorem: the Mayer–Vietoris sequences of two cohomology theories $H$ and $h$ joined by a natural map $\Phi$, here $h^q=H^q(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{R})$ and $\Phi=I$ (the proof of Poincaré duality on [[poincare-duality|Compact supports and Poincaré duality]] uses the same ladder with $h^q=(H^{n-q}_c)^*$ and $\Phi=PD$). If $\Phi$ is an isomorphism for $U$, $V$ and $U\cap V$, the five lemma makes it one for $U\cup V$.
blocks.alt: Two horizontal exact sequences, each with five terms: H^{q-1}(U) plus H^{q-1}(V), H^{q-1}(U cap V), H^q(U cup V), H^q(U) plus H^q(V), H^q(U cap V). Vertical arrows Phi join corresponding terms; the four outer ones are marked as isomorphisms and the middle one is the conclusion.

blocks.title: Why de Rham cohomology equals real singular cohomology
blocks.body: The theorem has several proofs, and papers cite whichever matches their tools.

items.label: Integration and induction
items.body: The proof above: integration over smooth chains is a natural map; it is an isomorphism on convex sets by the two Poincaré lemmas, and Mayer–Vietoris with the five lemma spreads it to finite covers, then (using an exhaustion function) to all manifolds.

items.label: Fine resolutions of sheaves
items.body: Lim (Theorem 2.2) compares two resolutions of the constant sheaf $\mathbb{R}$: by sheaves of smooth forms and by sheaves of smooth singular cochains. Both are acyclic (fine or soft), so both compute sheaf cohomology $H^*(M;\mathbb{R})$. Wikipedia presents the forms side the same way, with the Poincaré lemma giving exactness of the resolution and partitions of unity giving fineness.

items.label: Čech cohomology of a good cover
items.body: For a good cover, de Rham cohomology agrees with the Čech cohomology of the cover with real coefficients, which depends only on the combinatorics of which sets meet (the nerve). Wikipedia credits this version essentially to Weil (1952); Bott–Tu build it from the Čech–de Rham double complex, and Guillemin–Haine sketch it in §5.8.

items.label: Currents
items.body: Allowing forms with distributional coefficients (currents) gives a complex that also computes singular cohomology and contains chains themselves as currents of integration. The price is the product: currents cannot in general be multiplied, so this version does not see the ring structure.

blocks.title: Periods determine classes
blocks.body: A closed $k$-form $\omega$ on $M$ is exact if and only if $\int_z\omega=0$ for every smooth $k$-cycle $z$. More generally, the integration pairing $H^k(M)\times H_k(M;\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$ is perfect when $H_k(M;\mathbb{R})$ is finite dimensional, and for $k=1$ the criterion says that a closed $1$-form has a potential if and only if its line integrals around all closed loops vanish.

If all periods vanish, $I[\omega]=0$ as an element of $\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R})$; by injectivity of $I$, $[\omega]=0$. The converse is Stokes. For the perfect pairing: $$H^k(M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{R}}(H_k(M;\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{R})$$, which is the dual space. For $k=1$, every $1$-cycle is homologous to a sum of closed loops, which can be taken smooth.

blocks.title: Torsion is invisible: the Klein bottle and the projective plane
blocks.body: Using the integral homology computed on [[homology]], $H_1(K)\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2(K)=0$ for the Klein bottle and $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2)=0$, compute their de Rham cohomology, and explain why a closed form has zero integral over a cycle $c$ with $2c$ a boundary.
blocks.solution: By de Rham's theorem $H^k_{dR}=\operatorname{Hom}(H_k,\mathbb{R})$, and every homomorphism from a finite group to $\mathbb{R}$ is zero. So for the Klein bottle $H^0=\mathbb{R}$, $H^1=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{R})=\mathbb{R}$, $H^2=0$, the same as for a circle; for $\mathbb{RP}^2$, $H^0=\mathbb{R}$ and $H^1=H^2=0$, the same as for a point. (The vanishing of $H^2$ in both cases also matches non-orientability.) If $2c=\partial b$ and $\omega$ is closed, then $2\int_c\omega=\int_{\partial b}\omega=\int_bd\omega=0$. Kedlaya's notes give an algebraic instance: on an Enriques surface the canonical bundle defines a nontrivial $2$-torsion class in $H^2$, and like every torsion class it maps to zero in de Rham cohomology with real or complex coefficients.

blocks.title: Integral classes and quantised fluxes
blocks.body: The image of $H^k(M;\mathbb{Z})\to H^k(M;\mathbb{R})\cong H^k_{dR}(M)$ is called the lattice of integral classes. Show that a class is integral (in this image) exactly when all its periods over integral cycles are integers, assuming $H_k(M)$ finitely generated, and explain how this matches flux quantisation for a $2$-form $F$ with $\int_{S^2}F\in\mathbb{Z}$.
blocks.solution: With $H_k(M)\cong\mathbb{Z}^b\oplus T$, the universal coefficient theorem identifies the free part of $H^k(M;\mathbb{Z})$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^b,\mathbb{Z})$, and its image in $\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R})$ consists of the homomorphisms taking integer values on $\mathbb{Z}^b$ (torsion classes map to zero). Under $I$, this is the condition $\int_z\omega\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all integral cycles $z$. On $M=\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, $H_2=\mathbb{Z}$ generated by the unit sphere, so a closed $2$-form is integral exactly when its flux through $S^2$ is an integer. In the normalisation of Bhardwaj et al. ('t Hooft lines carry magnetic charge $q$ with $\int_{S^2}F=q\in\mathbb{Z}$), quantisation of magnetic flux is precisely the statement that $[F]$ is an integral class. Lim's discussion of the exponential sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{E}^\times\to0$ explains where integrality comes from for line bundles: smooth complex line bundles are classified by $H^2(X;\mathbb{Z})$, and the first Chern form represents the image of this integral class.

blocks.body:
- De Rham cohomology is real cohomology. It loses all torsion of $H^*(M;\mathbb{Z})$: the Klein bottle has $H^1_{dR}=\mathbb{R}$, like a circle, and $\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ has the de Rham cohomology of a point. Statements about integral classes (Chern classes in $H^2(M;\mathbb{Z})$, flux quantisation) need extra input beyond forms.
- Singular simplices are only continuous, and a form cannot be integrated over a continuous simplex. The smoothing theorem is a genuine step of the proof, not a formality.
- The isomorphism goes to cohomology, not homology: de Rham classes are functionals on cycles. On a compact oriented manifold [[poincare-duality|Poincaré duality]] identifies $H^k$ with the dual of $H^{n-k}$, hence, by de Rham's theorem, with $H_{n-k}(M;\mathbb{R})$, which is why papers sometimes blur the two, but on non-compact manifolds they differ.
- Homotopy invariance of de Rham cohomology does not require de Rham's theorem (it was proved directly above), but topological invariance under homeomorphisms that are not smooth does.

1. Show directly from the definitions that $I:H^0(M)\to H^0(M;\mathbb{R})$ is an isomorphism for every $M$.
2. Using $H_1(\Sigma_g)=\mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ for the closed orientable surface of genus $g$, compute $H^*_{dR}(\Sigma_g)$, and check [[poincare-duality|Poincaré duality]] and $\chi=2-2g$.
3. Let $\omega$ be a closed $1$-form on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{p,q\}$ with $\int_{\gamma_p}\omega=\int_{\gamma_q}\omega=0$. Show that $\omega$ is exact, and write $\omega_p-\omega_q$ plus an exact form for a form with periods $(2\pi,-2\pi)$.
4. For the nonorientable surface $N_k$ with $H_1(N_k)=\mathbb{Z}^{k-1}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2=0$, compute $H^*_{dR}(N_k)$.
5. Show that the class of the area form of $S^2$ divided by $4\pi$ is integral, and that the class of $\Phi/(4\pi)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$ (with $\Phi$ from the flux example) is a generator of the integral lattice.

blocks.title: Betti numbers and what they count
blocks.body:
For a manifold with finite-dimensional cohomology the Betti numbers $b_k=\dim H^k(M)$ are, by de Rham's theorem, the ranks of the integral homology groups of [[homology]], so the two pages' Betti numbers agree. Applied papers read them as counts of features. Su–Tong–Wei, who work with domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (compact $3$-manifolds with boundary carved out of a grid), interpret $b_0$ as the number of connected components, $b_1$ as the number of tunnels (independent loops that cannot be filled in) and $b_2$ as the number of cavities (enclosed voids). López Neumann gives the matching reading for open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$: $H^0$ counts components, $H^1$ measures curl-free fields that are not gradients (for example on $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a line), $H^2$ measures divergence-free fields that are not curls (for example on $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a point), and in general the failure reflects holes of the domain.

For a region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ these numbers are computed from forms: $b_1$ is the number of independent curl-free fields modulo gradients, and $b_2$ the number of independent divergence-free fields modulo curls.

blocks.title: Solid torus, spherical shell and their complements
blocks.body: Compute the Betti numbers of (a) an open solid torus $D$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, (b) the open spherical shell $\{1< |x|< 2\}$, (c) $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a closed solid torus, and identify representing forms or fields.
blocks.solution:
(a) $D$ deformation retracts onto its core circle, so $b=(1,1,0,0)$. A representative of $H^1$ is the angle form $(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2)$ around the axis through the hole (with the torus placed around the $z$-axis), restricted to $D$: one tunnel.

(b) The shell retracts onto $S^2$: $b=(1,0,1,0)$. The field $x/|x|^3$, as the $2$-form $\Phi$, represents $H^2$: one cavity.

(c) Let $W$ be the complement of a closed solid torus $\bar D$ and $D'$ a slightly larger open solid torus, so that $\mathbb{R}^3=W\cup D'$ and $W\cap D'$ is a thickened torus surface, homotopy equivalent to $T^2$. Since $H^k(\mathbb{R}^3)=0$ for $k\ge1$, the Mayer–Vietoris sequence breaks into isomorphisms $H^k(W)\oplus H^k(D')\cong H^k(T^2)$ for $k=1,2$ (and $H^3(W)=0$). With $H^1(D')=\mathbb{R}$, $H^2(D')=0$ and $b(T^2)=(1,2,1)$, this gives $b_1(W)=1$ and $b_2(W)=1$, so $b(W)=(1,1,1,0)$. The $H^1$ class is represented by the field of a steady current along the core circle of the torus (it circulates around the tube; its integral around a small meridian loop is nonzero), and the $H^2$ class by the flux of a field with a point source inside $\bar D$ through the boundary torus.

blocks.title: Sheaves and Čech cohomology
blocks.body:
Complex geometry papers such as Lim's survey use de Rham cohomology through sheaf theory (see [[sheaves]] and [[sheaf-cohomology]]). The dictionary is short.

Let $\underline{\mathbb{R}}$ be the sheaf of locally constant real functions and $\mathcal{E}^k$ the sheaf $U\mapsto\Omega^k(U)$. The sequence of sheaves
$$0\to\underline{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathcal{E}^0\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{E}^1\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{E}^2\to\cdots$$
is exact, because exactness of sheaves is a local condition and locally it is the Poincaré lemma on balls (plus $H^0$ of a ball being the constants). So it is a resolution of $\underline{\mathbb{R}}$. Each $\mathcal{E}^k$ is fine (it admits partitions of unity), and fine sheaves on paracompact spaces have no higher cohomology. A resolution by such acyclic sheaves computes sheaf cohomology from global sections, so
$$H^k(M;\underline{\mathbb{R}})\cong H^k\big(\Omega^*(M),d\big)=H^k_{dR}(M).$$
The same mechanism, with the sheaf of smooth singular cochains, gives de Rham's theorem in Lim's Theorem 2.2; with the holomorphic forms $\Omega^p$ resolved by smooth $(p,q)$-forms it gives Dolbeault's theorem (Lim, Theorem 2.3), which is outside this page.

Čech side. For an open cover $\mathfrak{U}=\{U_\alpha\}$, a Čech $p$-cochain with real coefficients assigns a real number $c_{\alpha_0\cdots\alpha_p}$ to each ordered $(p+1)$-tuple with $U_{\alpha_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{\alpha_p}\ne\varnothing$, alternating in the indices, with coboundary $(\delta c)_{\alpha_0\cdots\alpha_{p+1}}=\sum_i(-1)^ic_{\alpha_0\cdots\widehat{\alpha_i}\cdots\alpha_{p+1}}$. For a good cover this is the simplicial cochain complex of the nerve (the simplicial complex with a vertex for each $U_\alpha$ and a $p$-simplex for each nonempty $(p+1)$-fold intersection). Bott–Tu (Chapter II, §8) prove, with the Čech–de Rham double complex and the Mayer–Vietoris principle for many open sets, that for a good cover $H^*_{dR}(M)\cong\check H^*(\mathfrak{U};\mathbb{R})$; Guillemin–Haine (§5.8) sketch the same argument for manifolds of finite topology. We state this without proof.

blocks.title: The circle from the nerve of a three-arc cover
blocks.body: Cover $S^1$ by three open arcs $U_0,U_1,U_2$, each slightly more than a third of the circle, so that consecutive arcs overlap in an arc and the triple intersection is empty. Compute the Čech cohomology of this cover.
blocks.solution: Each $U_i$ and each nonempty $U_i\cap U_j$ is an arc, so the cover is good. The nerve has $3$ vertices and the $3$ edges $\{0,1\},\{0,2\},\{1,2\}$, and no triangle: it is the hollow triangle of [[homology]]. Čech $0$-cochains are $\mathbb{R}^3$, $1$-cochains $\mathbb{R}^3$, and $\delta:C^0\to C^1$, $(\delta c)_{ij}=c_j-c_i$, is the transpose of the boundary matrix $\partial_1$ of the hollow triangle, of rank $2$. So $\check H^0=\ker\delta=\mathbb{R}$ (constant cochains) and $\check H^1=\mathbb{R}^3/\operatorname{im}\delta=\mathbb{R}$, in agreement with $H^*_{dR}(S^1)$.

blocks.title: Harmonic forms and the Hodge decomposition
blocks.body:
A Riemannian metric picks out a best representative in each cohomology class. Full proofs belong to [[hodge-theory]]; here are the definitions and statements in the form papers use them, following Su–Tong–Wei's preliminaries.

Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian $m$-manifold with volume form $\mu$. The metric gives an inner product $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$ on $k$-forms at each point (the one for which $dx_I$, $|I|=k$, is orthonormal when $dx_1,\dots,dx_m$ is). The Hodge star $\star:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{m-k}$ is defined by
$$\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\mu,$$
and on a compact $M$ the $L^2$ inner product is $(\alpha,\beta)=\int_M\alpha\wedge\star\beta$. In $\mathbb{R}^m$ with the Euclidean metric, $\star dx_I=\pm dx_{I^c}$ with the sign making $dx_I\wedge\star dx_I=\mu$; for instance in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $\star dx=dy\wedge dz$, $\star dy=dz\wedge dx$, $\star dz=dx\wedge dy$, and $\star\star=(-1)^{k(m-k)}$ on $k$-forms. The codifferential on $k$-forms is
$$\delta=(-1)^{m(k-1)+1}\star d\star:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{k-1},$$
the formal adjoint of $d$: $(d\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha,\delta\beta)$ on a closed manifold. The Hodge Laplacian is $\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$, and $\omega$ is harmonic if $\Delta\omega=0$. On a closed manifold, $(\Delta\omega,\omega)=\|d\omega\|^2+\|\delta\omega\|^2$, so harmonic means $d\omega=0$ and $\delta\omega=0$ (Su–Tong–Wei, Eq. 7). For functions on $\mathbb{R}^m$, $\Delta f=-\sum_i\partial_i^2f$, the analyst's Laplacian with the opposite sign.

blocks.title: Hodge theorem (statement)
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be a closed (compact, no boundary) oriented Riemannian manifold and $\mathcal{H}^k$ the space of harmonic $k$-forms. Then
$$\Omega^k(M)=d\Omega^{k-1}(M)\oplus\delta\Omega^{k+1}(M)\oplus\mathcal{H}^k,$$
an $L^2$-orthogonal direct sum, and the map $\mathcal{H}^k\to H^k(M)$, $\omega\mapsto[\omega]$, is an isomorphism. So every de Rham class contains exactly one harmonic form, $\dim\mathcal{H}^k=b_k$, and the harmonic representative is the unique form of least $L^2$ norm in its class. The proof of the decomposition (elliptic regularity) is on [[hodge-theory]]; Lim's survey proves it as the first step towards the Kodaira embedding theorem. The norm statement follows from the decomposition, as shown next.

blocks.title: Proof that harmonic representatives minimise the norm
blocks.body: Assume the decomposition. A closed form $\omega$ is orthogonal to $\delta\Omega^{k+1}$, since $(\omega,\delta\beta)=(d\omega,\beta)=0$; so $\omega=d\alpha+h$ with $h$ harmonic, and $[\omega]=[h]$. If $h,h'$ are harmonic and cohomologous, $h-h'=d\alpha$ is both harmonic and exact, hence orthogonal to itself: $(d\alpha,d\alpha)=(\alpha,\delta(h-h'))=0$. For minimality, $$\|h+d\alpha\|^2=\|h\|^2+2(h,d\alpha)+\|d\alpha\|^2=\|h\|^2+\|d\alpha\|^2$$, because $(h,d\alpha)=(\delta h,\alpha)=0$.

items.label: Best representative
items.body: Each class on a compact oriented Riemannian manifold contains exactly one harmonic form, and it is the one of least $L^2$ norm (least energy). A class, an abstract coset, becomes a concrete form once a metric is chosen.

items.label: Orthogonal splitting
items.body: Su–Tong–Wei use the Hodge decomposition itself: any form splits uniquely and orthogonally into exact, coexact and harmonic parts, the vector-calculus version being gradient plus curl plus a harmonic field, and the harmonic part is the topological signal.

items.label: Kernel of a matrix
items.body: After discretisation (their §3) harmonic forms are null vectors of a sparse symmetric matrix, the discrete Hodge Laplacian, and Betti numbers are nullities; persistence tracks these nullities along a filtration.

items.label: Gateway to complex geometry
items.body: Lim's survey treats the isomorphism between harmonic forms and de Rham cohomology as the analytic input from which, on Kähler manifolds, the Hodge decomposition and eventually the Kodaira embedding theorem are derived.

blocks.title: Harmonic representatives on the circle and the flat torus
blocks.body: (a) On $S^1$ with the metric $d\theta^2$, find the harmonic representative of the class of $g(\theta)\,d\theta$. (b) On the flat torus $T^n=\mathbb{R}^n/2\pi\mathbb{Z}^n$, show that the forms with constant coefficients in $d\theta_I$ are harmonic.
blocks.solution:
(a) Here $m=1$, $\star d\theta=1$ and $\star1=d\theta$. For a $1$-form, $\delta(g\,d\theta)=(-1)^{1\cdot0+1}\star d\star(g\,d\theta)=-\star dg=-g'$, and on functions $\delta=0$. So $\Delta(g\,d\theta)=d\delta(g\,d\theta)=-g''\,d\theta$, and $g\,d\theta$ is harmonic exactly when $g$ is constant ($g''=0$ and periodic). The class of $g\,d\theta$ is determined by $\int g$, so its harmonic representative is $\bar g\,d\theta$ with $\bar g=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}g$, and $g\,d\theta=\bar g\,d\theta+df$ with $f=\int_0^\theta(g-\bar g)$, as in the first example. The minimality is the inequality $\int_0^{2\pi}g^2\ge2\pi\bar g^2$, which is Cauchy–Schwarz.

(b) In flat coordinates the metric is Euclidean, $\star$ sends $d\theta_I$ to $\pm d\theta_{I^c}$ with constant coefficients, and $d$ of a constant-coefficient form is zero. So $d\omega=0$ and $\delta\omega=\pm\star d\star\omega=0$. There are $\binom nk$ independent such $k$-forms, which is $b_k(T^n)$, so by the Hodge theorem they are all the harmonic forms, and they represent the classes found by Künneth.

blocks.caption: A closed $1$-form $g(\theta)\,d\theta$ on the circle (blue coefficient) and its harmonic representative $\bar g\,d\theta$ (red, the mean value). The difference is $f'(\theta)\,d\theta$ for the periodic function $f$ (green), so the two forms are cohomologous; the harmonic one has the smallest $L^2$ norm in the class.
