blocks.title: Manifolds with boundary: absolute and relative cohomology
blocks.body:
Applied papers work on compact domains with boundary, and there the harmonic fields $\{\omega:d\omega=0,\ \delta\omega=0\}$ form an infinite-dimensional space (on a disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$, for instance, $u\,dx-v\,dy$ is closed and coclosed for every holomorphic function $u+iv$, by the Cauchy–Riemann equations). Su–Tong–Wei explain how boundary conditions cut it down. Integration by parts acquires a boundary term, $(d\omega,\eta)=(\omega,\delta\eta)+\int_{\partial M}\omega\wedge\star\eta$, and they introduce two subspaces:
- normal (Dirichlet) forms $\Omega^k_n=\{\omega:\ \omega|_{\partial M}=0\}$, meaning the pullback of $\omega$ to $\partial M$ vanishes;
- tangential (Neumann) forms $\Omega^k_t=\{\omega:\ \star\omega|_{\partial M}=0\}$.

$d$ preserves the normal condition and $\delta$ the tangential one, and $\star$ exchanges them. The normal forms form a subcomplex whose cohomology is the relative de Rham cohomology $H^k(M,\partial M)$, and the space $\mathcal{H}^k_n$ of harmonic fields with normal boundary condition is isomorphic to it, with dimension $b_{m-k}$; the harmonic fields with tangential boundary condition $\mathcal{H}^k_t$ are isomorphic to the absolute cohomology $H^k(M)$, of dimension $b_k$. They also quote the Hodge–Morrey decomposition $\Omega^k=d\Omega^{k-1}_n\oplus\delta\Omega^{k+1}_t\oplus\mathcal{H}^k$ and its refinement, the Hodge–Morrey–Friedrichs decomposition. (In the paragraph after their Remark 2 the definition of $\mathcal{H}^k_t$ is misprinted as $\mathcal{H}^k_t\cap\Omega^k_t$; the intended space is the harmonic fields lying in $\Omega^k_t$, as in the normal case.) Proofs are not covered here; see the references in Su–Tong–Wei, §2.1.

blocks.title: The interval
blocks.body: For $M=[0,1]$ compute the absolute cohomology $H^*(M)$, the relative cohomology $H^*(M,\partial M)$ from the complex of normal forms, and check the dimensions $b_k$ and $b_{m-k}$.
blocks.solution: Absolute: $H^0=\mathbb{R}$ (constants) and every $f\,dx$ is exact, so $H^1=0$; $b=(1,0)$. Relative: the normal $0$-forms are the functions vanishing at $0$ and $1$; the pullback of a $1$-form to the boundary points is automatically $0$, so all $1$-forms are normal. Closed normal $0$-forms are constants vanishing at the ends, so $H^0(M,\partial M)=0$. A $1$-form $f\,dx$ is $dg$ with $g(0)=g(1)=0$ if and only if $\int_0^1f=0$ (take $g(x)=\int_0^xf$), so $H^1(M,\partial M)\cong\mathbb{R}$ via $\int_0^1$. The dimensions are $(0,1)=(b_{1-0},b_{1-1})$, as stated. Harmonic fields: on $[0,1]$ they are the constant functions and the constant multiples of $dx$. The normal condition kills the constant functions and keeps $dx$, so $\mathcal{H}^*_n$ has dimensions $(0,1)$; the tangential condition asks that $\star\omega$ pull back to zero at the endpoints, which is automatic for functions ($\star1=dx$) and forces $c=0$ for $c\,dx$ ($\star(c\,dx)=c$), so $\mathcal{H}^*_t$ has dimensions $(1,0)$, matching $H^*(M)$.

blocks.title: Codifferential and Hodge star signs
blocks.body: The sign in front of $\star d\star$ varies with how it is written; in Riemannian signature the common versions agree. Check against adjointness, $(d\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha,\delta\beta)$, which fixes $\delta$ uniquely.

rows.text: Since $m(k-1)$ and $m(k+1)$ differ by $2m$, the same operator is $(-1)^{m(k+1)+1}\star d\star$; and since $\star\star=(-1)^{j(m-j)}$ on $j$-forms in Riemannian signature, it is also $(-1)^k\star^{-1}d\star$. All three are one operator.

In general signature the definition of $\delta$ carries an extra factor $s$, the sign (parity) of the signature of the metric, and $\star\star=s(-1)^{k(m-k)}$; in Lorentzian physics papers this changes signs relative to the Riemannian formulas.
$\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$ is a nonnegative operator; on functions in $\mathbb{R}^m$ it is $-\sum\partial_i^2$, the negative of the usual analyst's Laplacian.

blocks.title: Discrete de Rham complexes
blocks.body:
Numerical analysts and topological data analysts replace forms by cochains on a mesh, and the de Rham complex by the simplicial cochain complex. The bridge is integration. For a simplicial (or cubical) complex $K$ triangulating a domain, the de Rham map $\mathcal{R}:\Omega^k\to C^k(K;\mathbb{R})$ records the integrals of a $k$-form over the oriented $k$-cells, $(\mathcal{R}\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega$; Su–Tong–Wei store a discrete $k$-form as exactly this vector of integrals. The discrete exterior derivative $D_k:C^k\to C^{k+1}$ is the transpose of the boundary matrix $\partial_{k+1}$ of [[homology]], so $D_{k+1}D_k=0$ because $\partial\partial=0$, and Stokes' theorem on each cell is the commuting relation
$$D_k\,\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}\,d,\qquad\text{since}\quad(\mathcal{R}d\omega)(\tau)=\int_\tau d\omega=\int_{\partial\tau}\omega=(\mathcal{R}\omega)(\partial\tau).$$
Guzmán–Hirani–Liu–Potu use this together with the Whitney map $W$ from cochains to piecewise polynomial forms, which satisfies $dW=WD$ and $\mathcal{R}W=\mathrm{id}$ (they refer to Whitney's book for both), so cochains can be turned back into genuine forms without changing the cohomology. Their discrete Poincaré operators are built from cone operators on chains: a map $\mathrm{Co}$ raising dimension by one with
$$\mathrm{Co}(\partial\sigma)+\partial\,\mathrm{Co}(\sigma)=\sigma\ (\dim\sigma\ge1),\qquad\partial\,\mathrm{Co}(v)=v-a\ \ (\text{vertices}),$$
for a fixed vertex $a$; on a complex that is star-shaped with respect to $a$, $\mathrm{Co}[v_0,\dots,v_k]=[a,v_0,\dots,v_k]$ (zero if $a$ is already a vertex of the simplex). The dual operator $P$ on cochains, $(P\alpha)(\sigma)=\alpha(\mathrm{Co}\,\sigma)$, satisfies $DP+PD=\mathrm{id}$ on cochains of positive degree, the discrete counterpart of $dK+Kd=\mathrm{id}$.

Hodge theory becomes linear algebra. Su–Tong–Wei use diagonal discrete Hodge stars $S_k$ (ratios of dual to primal cell volumes) and the discrete Laplacian $L_k=D_k^{\mathsf T}S_{k+1}D_k+S_kD_{k-1}S_{k-1}^{-1}D_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}S_k$; replacing all stars by identities gives $L^B_k=D_k^{\mathsf T}D_k+D_{k-1}D_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}$, with the same kernel dimensions. In every version, $\dim\ker L_k=b_k$ of the complex: the discrete Hodge theorem, which in finite dimensions is just the orthogonal decomposition $C^k=\operatorname{im}D_{k-1}\oplus\operatorname{im}D_k^{\mathsf T}\oplus\ker L_k$.

blocks.title: Betti numbers as kernels of Laplacian matrices
blocks.body: Compute $\ker L^B_k$ for the hollow triangle (three vertices, three edges) and for the boundary of a tetrahedron, and compare with the Betti numbers from [[homology]].
blocks.solution:
Hollow triangle, edges ordered $[0,1],[0,2],[1,2]$: $D_0=\partial_1^{\mathsf T}$ has rows $(-1,1,0)$, $(-1,0,1)$, $(0,-1,1)$. Then $L^B_0=D_0^{\mathsf T}D_0$ is the graph Laplacian $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&-1\\-1&2&-1\\-1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, with kernel the constants: $\dim=1=b_0$. There are no $2$-cells, so $L^B_1=D_0D_0^{\mathsf T}$, a $3\times3$ matrix of rank $2$, with kernel spanned by $(1,-1,1)$, the cochain $[0,1]-[0,2]+[1,2]$ dual to the cycle $z$ of [[homology]]: $\dim=1=b_1$.

Tetrahedron boundary ($4$ vertices, $6$ edges, $4$ triangles): $\operatorname{rank}D_0=3$ and $\operatorname{rank}D_1=3$, so $\dim\ker L^B_0=4-3=1$, $\dim\ker L^B_1=6-3-3=0$, $\dim\ker L^B_2=4-3=1$. These are $b=(1,0,1)$ of the sphere. In general $\dim\ker L_k=\dim C^k-\operatorname{rank}D_k-\operatorname{rank}D_{k-1}$, which is $\dim\ker D_k-\dim\operatorname{im}D_{k-1}$.

blocks.title: A discrete Poincaré operator on a triangle
blocks.body: On the filled triangle with vertices $0,1,2$ and cone vertex $a=0$, write down $\mathrm{Co}$, check the cone identity, and use $P$ to find a $0$-cochain $\beta$ with $D\beta=\alpha$ for the closed $1$-cochain $\alpha$ with values $\alpha[0,1]=2$, $\alpha[0,2]=5$, $\alpha[1,2]=3$.
blocks.solution:
$\mathrm{Co}[0]=0$, $\mathrm{Co}[1]=[0,1]$, $\mathrm{Co}[2]=[0,2]$, $\mathrm{Co}[1,2]=[0,1,2]$, and $\mathrm{Co}[0,1]=\mathrm{Co}[0,2]=0$ (degenerate). Check on $[1,2]$: $\partial\mathrm{Co}[1,2]=[1,2]-[0,2]+[0,1]$ and $\mathrm{Co}\,\partial[1,2]=\mathrm{Co}([2]-[1])=[0,2]-[0,1]$, with sum $[1,2]$. On $[0,1]$: $\mathrm{Co}\,\partial[0,1]=\mathrm{Co}([1]-[0])=[0,1]$. On vertices, $\partial\mathrm{Co}[v]=v-[0]$.

$\alpha$ is closed: $(D\alpha)[0,1,2]=\alpha(\partial[0,1,2])=\alpha[1,2]-\alpha[0,2]+\alpha[0,1]=3-5+2=0$. Put $\beta=P\alpha$: $\beta[0]=\alpha(0)=0$, $\beta[1]=\alpha[0,1]=2$, $\beta[2]=\alpha[0,2]=5$. Then $D\beta[0,1]=\beta[1]-\beta[0]=2$, $D\beta[0,2]=5$, $D\beta[1,2]=3$: $D\beta=\alpha$. This is the discrete version of integrating a closed $1$-form along rays from the cone point.

blocks.title: Curvature and characteristic classes
blocks.body:
The most frequent source of de Rham classes in geometry and physics is curvature. The full theory is on [[curvature-forms]] (with [[vector-bundles]]); what papers assume from this page is the following mechanism. A connection on a complex vector bundle $E$ of rank $r$ is described, over an open set where $E$ has a frame, by an $r\times r$ matrix $\theta$ of $1$-forms; its curvature is the matrix of $2$-forms $\Theta=d\theta+\theta\wedge\theta$ (Lim, Proposition 2.10, writes $\Theta=d\theta+\theta^2$; Notman–Sanabani write $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$). Under a change of frame $\Theta$ is conjugated, so invariant polynomials of $\Theta$, such as $\operatorname{tr}\Theta^k$ or the coefficients of $\det(I+t\Theta)$, are globally defined forms. Two facts make them cohomology classes:
1. They are closed. This follows from the Bianchi identity $d\Theta=\Theta\wedge\theta-\theta\wedge\Theta$ (Lim, Proposition 2.11, $d\Theta=[\Theta,\theta]$): for instance $$d\operatorname{tr}\Theta^k=k\operatorname{tr}(d\Theta\wedge\Theta^{k-1})=k\operatorname{tr}([\Theta,\theta]\Theta^{k-1})=0$$, a trace of a graded commutator.
2. Their classes do not depend on the connection (Notman–Sanabani, Corollary 2.90; Lim states it as Proposition 2.16 and only indicates the interpolation argument). Wikipedia's proof is by homotopy invariance: join two connections by the path $\theta_t=(1-t)\theta_0+t\theta_1$, regard it as one connection on $E\times\mathbb{R}\to M\times\mathbb{R}$, and pull back along the inclusions at $t=0$ and $t=1$, which are homotopic.

For a line bundle ($r=1$) everything is scalar and can be checked by hand, as in the next example. The resulting classes are the Chern classes; their normalisations differ between sources.

blocks.title: Line bundles: closed curvature, connection-independent class
blocks.body: For a complex line bundle, a connection is given by local $1$-forms $\theta_\alpha$ on a cover, with $\theta_\beta=\theta_\alpha+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$ for the transition functions $g_{\alpha\beta}$ (Lim's frame-change rule for $r=1$). Show that the curvature $\Theta=d\theta_\alpha$ is a well-defined closed $2$-form, and that changing the connection changes $\Theta$ by an exact form.
blocks.solution: For $r=1$, $\theta\wedge\theta=0$, so $\Theta=d\theta_\alpha$ locally. On overlaps $d\theta_\beta-d\theta_\alpha=d(g^{-1}dg)=d(d\log g)=0$ locally (where a branch of $\log g$ exists; in general $d(g^{-1}dg)=-g^{-2}dg\wedge dg=0$), so the local forms agree and $\Theta$ is global. It is closed, being locally exact. For a second connection $\theta'_\alpha$, the differences $a=\theta'_\alpha-\theta_\alpha$ agree on overlaps (the $g^{-1}dg$ terms cancel), so $a$ is a global $1$-form and $\Theta'-\Theta=da$ is exact. Hence $[\Theta]\in H^2(M;\mathbb{C})$ depends only on the bundle. With Lim's normalisation, $c_1(L)=\big[\tfrac{\sqrt{-1}}{2\pi}\Theta\big]$; it is the image of an integral class (the exponential sequence), so its integral over every closed oriented surface is an integer. Note that $\Theta$ itself is only locally exact: $[\Theta]$ is the obstruction to finding one global $\theta$.

blocks.title: Normalising Chern classes
blocks.body: These conventions change signs and factors of $2\pi$ and $i$ in formulas that papers quote without comment.

rows.text: $c(E)=\det\big(I+\tfrac{\sqrt{-1}}{2\pi}\Theta\big)$, the $k$-th Chern form being its degree-$2k$ part; so $c_1=\tfrac{\sqrt{-1}}{2\pi}\operatorname{tr}\Theta$.

$c_k=\varepsilon_k(F)/(2\pi i)^k$ (their Example 2.93), where $\det(I+tA)=\sum_kt^k\varepsilon_k(A)$ (Definition 2.91) and $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$ as in Lim. blocks.title: Closed forms in physics
blocks.body:
Bhardwaj et al.'s lectures on generalised symmetries assume this page's material under a physics dictionary. Spacetime is a $d$-manifold.
- A conserved current for a continuous symmetry is a closed $(d-1)$-form $j$ (the Hodge dual of a divergence-free vector current); for a $p$-form symmetry it is a closed $(d-p-1)$-form.
- The symmetry operator on a closed oriented submanifold $\Sigma$ is $U_g(\Sigma)=\exp\big(i\alpha\int_\Sigma j\big)$. It is topological: deforming $\Sigma$ to $\Sigma'$ with $\Sigma-\Sigma'=\partial\Sigma_d$ changes the exponent by $\int_{\Sigma_d}dj=0$. So charges are periods of closed forms, and only the homology class of $\Sigma$ matters.
- In Maxwell theory $F=dA$ locally, the Bianchi identity $dF=0$ gives a magnetic symmetry with current $F$, and the equation of motion $d\star F=0$ an electric one with current $\star F$. Gauge transformations shift $A$ by exact forms, $A\mapsto A-\frac{1}{2\pi}d\theta$ in their normalisation, which leave $F$ unchanged.
- Fluxes through closed surfaces are quantised: in their normalisation $\int_{S^2}F=q\in\mathbb{Z}$ around an 't Hooft line, so $[F]$ is an integral class in the sense of the de Rham section, and the field of a monopole is a closed, non-exact form on the complement of its worldline, like $\Phi$ above.
- A charged defect on $M_p$ appears in the conservation law as $dj=q\,\delta(M_p)$, the [[poincare-duality|Poincaré dual]] delta-form; linking of $\Sigma$ with $M_p$ then gives the phase $e^{iq\alpha}$ by Stokes.
- In discrete gauge theories, forms are replaced by cochains and wedge products by cup products, with actions such as $2\pi\int a\cup\delta b$, the cochain analogue of $B\wedge dA$.

blocks.title: Charge measured on any enclosing surface
blocks.body: In $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ (a time slice), a static point charge at the origin gives the electric flux form $\star E=\frac{q}{4\pi}\Phi$ with $\Phi$ from the flux example. Show that the charge measured by $\int_\Sigma\star E$ is $q$ for every closed surface $\Sigma$ enclosing the origin once (homologous to the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$) and $0$ for surfaces not enclosing it, and phrase the source equation with a delta-form.
blocks.solution: $\Phi$ is closed on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, and $H_2(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\})=\mathbb{Z}$ is generated by the unit sphere $S$. If $\Sigma$ is homologous to $S$, then $\Sigma-S=\partial c$ for a $3$-chain $c$ avoiding the origin, and $\int_\Sigma\Phi-\int_S\Phi=\int_cd\Phi=0$, so $\int_\Sigma\star E=\frac q{4\pi}4\pi=q$. A surface not enclosing the origin bounds in $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, so the integral is $0$. On all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, $d\star E$ is not zero but concentrated at the origin: $d\star E=q\,\delta^3(x)$, where $\delta^3$ is the $3$-form [[poincare-duality|Poincaré dual]] to the point (the delta function times $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$), and Stokes on a ball $B$ around the origin gives $\int_{\partial B}\star E=\int_Bq\,\delta^3=q$, the same answer.

1. In $\mathbb{R}^3$, the magnetic field of a steady current along the $z$-axis is represented by the $1$-form $\frac{I}{2\pi}d\varphi$ (angle around the axis) for the field $B$ itself. Show that it is closed but not exact on the complement of the axis, and compute its period on a loop around the axis.
2. Show that if $A$ and $A'$ are two potentials for the same $F$ on a manifold $M$, then $A'-A$ is closed, and that it is exact if $H^1(M)=0$; describe the extra possible gauge fields on $S^1\times\mathbb{R}^3$.
3. Explain why the charge operator $U_g(\Sigma)$ depends only on $[\Sigma]\in H_{d-1}$ of the complement of the charged operators.

blocks.body: The same object is used for different jobs in the papers this page prepares for.

items.label: Numerical analysis
items.body: A complex of finite element spaces (Whitney forms) with commuting maps to and from cochains; potentials of closed forms are produced by explicit Poincaré and Bogovskiĭ operators that preserve boundary conditions, and vanishing of cohomology is certified at the level of cochains.

items.label: Topological data analysis
items.body: Betti numbers of a shape are read off as kernel dimensions of discrete Hodge Laplacians, with boundary conditions selecting absolute or relative cohomology, and tracked along filtrations (persistence).

items.label: Field theory
items.body: Conserved currents are closed forms, charges are their periods, topological invariance is Stokes' theorem, gauge freedom is the addition of exact forms, and flux quantisation is integrality of classes.

items.label: Arithmetic geometry
items.body: Algebraic de Rham cohomology gives a $K$-rational structure on complex cohomology; comparing it with the rational Betti structure produces periods, and the transcendence of periods is the subject of the de Rham–Betti and period conjectures.

items.label: Symplectic geometry
items.body: Equivariantly closed forms built from symplectic forms and moment maps have integrals computed exactly by fixed points (Atiyah–Bott, Duistermaat–Heckman).

blocks.body:
- Coefficients matter. De Rham cohomology of a manifold is over $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$ for complex forms, with $H^k(M;\mathbb{C})=H^k(M)\otimes\mathbb{C}$). Algebraic de Rham cohomology over $K$ has its own rational structure, different from the Betti one by periods; in characteristic $p$ it behaves differently again.
- Explicit formulas (for $d$ in terms of vector fields, for $\delta$, for Chern forms, for $d_G$) depend on normalisations; the cohomology groups do not. Check a paper's conventions against one computed example before reusing its constants.
- On manifolds with boundary, "harmonic" without a boundary condition does not give finite-dimensional spaces; papers mean harmonic with normal or tangential conditions, matching relative or absolute cohomology.
- $H^k(M)$ for non-compact $M$ can be infinite dimensional (for example the plane with infinitely many punctures, or $\mathbb{R}^2$ minus the integer lattice points). The finiteness results need a finite good cover.

This page rests on [[differential-forms]] (forms, $d$, pullback, Stokes' theorem) and [[homology]] (chains, cycles, Betti numbers). The next page, [[poincare-duality|Compact supports and Poincaré duality]], continues it directly with compactly supported cohomology, the compact Poincaré lemma, Poincaré duality and Poincaré duals of submanifolds.

On [[hodge-theory]], the harmonic representatives of this page become the starting point: on a compact Kähler manifold they split by type, giving the Hodge decomposition $H^k(M;\mathbb{C})=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}$, and the [[hodge|Hodge conjecture]] asks which rational classes of type $(p,p)$ come from subvarieties. On [[curvature-forms]], the mechanism of the characteristic-class section is developed in general (Chern–Weil theory), with Chern classes and their relatives; the [[gauss-bonnet]] theorem is the first instance of a curvature integral computing a topological number. The Čech–de Rham double complex leads to [[spectral-sequences]], developed in the later chapters of Bott–Tu; [[sheaf-cohomology]] puts the sheaf view of this page in general form, and [[morse-theory]] bounds the same Betti numbers by counts of critical points of a function. Integral refinements and torsion lead to [[cohomology]] with integer coefficients and to [[k-theory]]; equivariant cohomology and moment maps belong to [[symplectic-geometry]]; the physics dictionary continues in [[yang-mills]].

Equivariant de Rham cohomology (the Cartan model, equivariant integration and the localisation formula) will be treated on a planned page, Equivariant cohomology and localisation. Algebraic de Rham cohomology, its comparison with Betti cohomology and the period criterion for de Rham–Betti classes will be treated on a planned page, Algebraic de Rham cohomology and periods.
